speechtext: As my hon. friend is quoting me, I may say that it made no difference in the debt statement. It would make a difference in the surplus of the year, but not as affecting the debt statement of the year.

The hon. gentleman, when 1 was questioning the Minister of Railways about his system of charging, and showing how unjust it was and how it misrepresented the profits and losses of the year said :	What difference does it make ?
The hon. gentleman's point was, of course, that it all had to come out of the country. But are not the people entitled to know the truth ? Are we to be be-fooled into the belief that these railways are worked at a profit when they are worked at a loss ? Are we to be asked year after year to vote money for the maintenance of these railways under the belief that they are worked at a profit, when, as a matter of fact, they are worked at an enormous loss ? Why, hon. gentlemen opposite in the general election on every hustings in the country proclaimed the great ability of the Minister of Railways, and declared that he had made profits where others had made nothing but loss, that he had drawn order out of chaos. We want the people to know that he made no profits at all, but that, like others, he had done the work at a loss. I saw in ' Hansard ' that the hon. gentleman had said that hon. members on this side had unduly criticised his estimates. Surely,

what we have heard here justifies criticism. There is not an lion, member on this side, I do not think there is an lion, member in the House who will deny even the last dollar that may reasonably be asked for the maintenance of the Intercolonial Railway. Every dollar that can be fairly asked for will be given, whether the road is worked at a profit or at a loss. But let us know the truth about it. There is another feature showing the lamentable consequences of the hon. minister neglecting his repairs. Last year he had the grandest year in the history of the road. His gross revenue was $4,552.000. He had a great increase of traffic, as had every other road in the country. The railways did not need to seek for traffic-it flowed in upon them. The gross receipts showed an increase of $815,000, as against the previous year-largely passenger traffic. As to that increased passenger traffic, almost the whole of it was clear profit-extra people travelling in the trains. As to the freight, that would simply mean extra cars upon trains. It is not too much to say that it would not cost more than 40 per cent to work it. That is to say, he should have had 00 per cent profit on this $813,ouO increase, or not less than $500,000 cash profit. What a magnificent opportunity for the hon. gentleman to come before the country and claim a surplus. But he had been neglecting his track, he had been neglecting his cars, he had been neglecting his locomotives. And so, though he had $813,000, of which $500,000 ought to have been profit, yet his expenses, owing to his own neglect in previous years went up by $755,000. So, out of the whole $813,000, the hon. gentleman only got a beggarly $58,000. That is the result of the hon. gentleman scamping the repairs in previous years. Reference was' made, I think by the Finance Minister, to the present year as not being so successful as previous years. There is no doubt about that. The hon. gentleman in pursuance of his duty sends out every ten days a comparative statement of the revenues from all sources. We find that up to the 10th of May last year, the hon. gentleman showed a surplus from the, railways of $240,000. But this year at the same date he has a deficit of $497,000. Coming from the Finance Minister, I think we may take it as fairly accurate. So, against a surplus for 1900, we have a deficit for 1901, and the difference between the two years amounts to $737,000. I do not wonder that the hon. gentleman admits that it is not a good year. The hon. Minister of Railways will not be able to explain it away. He has* a great remedy in his capital charges. But I do not think that even that will help him on this occasion.

I desire to say that I have never understood it to be the practice of an opposition to call for separate votes on different items. It is considered quite sufficient for the opposition of the day to make a fair criticism of those items, and to show wherein they are uncalled for, wherein they are too large. But I say it is not the practice of an opposition, at least it has not been since I have been in this House, to challenge by vote the individual items separately. I am quite sure it was not ihe practice of lion, gentlemen opposite when they were in opposition. Now, the only matter I desire to refer to is with reference to the surplus. If there is any one thing that is misunderstood in this country it is certainly this bug-a-boo of a surplus. There are many people w'ho actually believe that the government have a large revenue over all their expenditure. An ordinary reader of the speech delivered by the Minister of Finance this afternoon would come to the conclusion flint we had last year a revenue of about eight million dollars over every dollar that we expended. This is owing to the system of book-keeping that is adopted in the Finance Department, a system of charging certain items to capital account and others to revenue account, without making the whole question plain to the ordinary reader. Had the precedent laid down by the former government been continued, and the same class of items charged to capital account as were formerly charged. so that a fair comparison could be made. I would not find so much fault with what is done now. But as has been shown conclusively by the hon. member for Hamilton who has just spoken, in the Railway Department the whole system has been changed, and charges that ,were heretofore made against revenue are now charged up to capital, so that the whole system is misleading to tlie general public. I think the time lias arrived when some new system of bookkeeping ought to be evolved by the Minister of Finance, by which the people could fairly understand the finances of the country. Therefore, I do not think it is fair to tlie electorate of this country that those who are in charge of tlie Finance Department should tell them that we had a surplus, when tlie revenue was actually a great deal less than the total expenditure. Last year our total revenue was only $51.031,400, showing a deficit of $1,080,000. Now, why should we continue this system of telling the people that we have a large surplus ? Is it not misleading ? I think it is. It is a bad system, and ought to be changed. The sooner the Minister of Finance changes his system and gives to the people a fair statement of the actual receipts and expenditures, the better will it be for the country. Not until then will the people get their eyes opened to the actual state of facts, and only then will they take those steps which are necessary to arrest the enormously increased expenditure that is going on year by year. Why. they are now asleep. The electors of the country are perfectly satisfied. They say. We have $8,000,000 of a surplus, what is the use of talking about extravagance ? We actually earned last year $8,000,000 more than we spent. The electorate are satisfied. But if you give them a fair and honest statement of the finances of this country, they will see that instead of a surplus we actually spent $1.(58(5.000 more than all the revenue last year,, and that by so much we have increased the national debt of the country. Then the eyes of the electorate will be opened, and then there will be a demand to arrest this enormously increased expendithre that is going on. Sir, not since the hon. gentlemen came into power have they had a surplus, although each year we are told they had a surplus. In three years out of tlie four for which

A full and complete statement of the total expenditure and the total revenue will show that we have a deficit and not a surplus, and then, and only then, will the people of this country grasp the idea that year by year we are going behind instead of going forward.

Before the motion for supply is adopted. I wish to make a remark or two concerning certain documents brought down in reply to addresses carried by this House in March last. As the House knows, I have often urged the bringing down of these documents. At one o'clock I received part of them.
There were two addresses voted on the same day-one for the correspondence between the Bi'itish government and the Canadian government concerning the commissions to be granted to Canadian officers in the British army ; and the other for the correspondence between the British and Canadian governments regarding the South African police force. Many documents were brought in reply to the first address-that relating to the commissions to be granted Canadian officers in the British army, including commissions that have been granted to Canadian officers in the West African police force. But, for what reason I do not know, not a single document has been brought down in response to the second motion. I do not suppose it could have been a very voluminous correspondence. Now. the position is this: I have moved for documents relating to a public question, a question of deep interest to the country, a question that has been discussed in political papers as well as in military organs, that has caused a great deal of comment throughout the country. The motion had in view to make public the conditions upon which these commissions were offered to Canadians. I wanted to know also whether the first steps were taken in England or in Canada-I think it is the right of parliament to have those documents. But. either His Excellency or the government has thought proper that all the documents should not be brought down. From what I have been able to learn from these documents since one o'clock, I think that the papers that are lacking are probably at Rideau Hal!. Among the documents produced, are several letters exchanged between Lord Minto and Mr. Chamberlain, and also letters between the Governor Gen- ' eral and Lord Roberts. Some of those documents refer to correspondence that does not appear here. For example, there is a telegram of the Oth April from Mr. Chamberlain to Lord Minto. referring to a previous telegram of the Oth April, and referring also to a special despatch called 'confidential,' dated 24th March. 1900, the contents of which the Colonial Secretary instructs the Governor General to communicate to his advisers. Either the contents of that despatch have been communicated to His Excellency's advisers, or they have not. Either the Governor General has carried out the orders of the Colonial Secretary. or he lias not. If lie lias not carried Mr. ROBINSON (West Elgin).
out those orders, the country should know it. If he has, the documents giving the precise instructions which he was to communicate to his advisers should have been brought before parliament. I may be told that there is a good deal of private correspondence exchanged between the Governor General and the Colonial Secretary. I know that the Governor General is not only the representative of the Crown in Canada, but also an official of the British government. I acknowledge that His Excellency has the right to exchange any private correspondence that he likes with the Colonial Office. But I do not acknowledge that the Governor General of Canada has the right to give instructions to the government of Canada, or the right to communicate them instructions from the Colonial Office, without bringing before the country all the documents on which those instructions are based. The time has passed when the government of this country can be carried on by private correspondence between Rideau Hall and Downing street. Whatever reasons the government may have for not bringing down this correspondence, parliament is entitled to know those reasons. And if there is private correspondence which resulted in inducing the government of Canada to supply Canadian soldiers to the British army, the word ' confidential ' ought to disappear, and the documents produced. The word did not prevent copies of some of those ' confidential ' documents of His Excellency being included among the papers that are sent to the House. Why not the others ? It is evident that there was some discussion between His Excellency and his advisers as to the authority which should recommend the Canadian officers to whom commissions were to be granted in the British army. I have made up my mind on that subject, and have expressed my opinion very clearly. I share entirely the opinion of the Canadian Military Gazette that the government of Canada should not have allowed the Imperial authorities to set on foot a movement in Canada to induce our officers to go there. It is plain from one of the documents that the commissions offered to the Canadian officers in the West African police are intended to lead to permanent employment in the British army. These officers are offered free transportation to Africa : they are to serve for some years on probation ; and they are offered leaves of absence to go to England and to return to Africa, but not to come to Canada. Therefore, the opinion of the Military Gazette, of which we had no proof up to this time, is well established, that this granting of commissions to Canadian officers in the Imperial army, especially in the West Africa police force, is simply a means of taking away Canadians for permanent residence in Africa. As a Canadian, notwithstanding what any one may

say as to the loyalty we owe to Great Britain, I hold that it is not the duty of the Governor General or his advisers to offer inducements to young Canadian officers to become settlers in Africa. We in Canada are making great sacrifices to keep our young men here, and also to bring settlers from outside, and we should not lend ourselves to any such movements as this that I have referred to. I go further : there are a number of commissions in the Imperial army offered to graduates of the Kingston Royal Military College. I have no objection to any Canadian officer going of his own free will to servo in the British army. But I do object to the government of Canada using the public money to promote his going. For what purpose was this college established, and for what purpose do we keep it up ? To educate young Canadians in military science. Then you get a staff of officers who can take command of our militia, so that when we need officers to command our soldiers for the defence of the country we shall have them. But now at the close of every course of study at Kingston, British officers will be allowed to come here and take the best of our officers, the best or our militiamen, and enlist them in the British service in Africa and elsewhere, a service that will become permanent, as said in the despatch from Lord Minto to Mr. Chamberlain. I am willing that the majority of this House should say, if they like, that Canada should continue to assist the British Empire when in danger. I respect the opinion of the majority when they say that in the hour of danger Canada should go to the help of the British Empire ; but I deny to any member of this House, if he is faithful to his duty as a representative of Canada, the right to tax the Canadian people in order to educate a staff of officers for the British army. They pay heavily in England for supporting their own army and educating their own officers. We do not ask the people of England to help us pay for our militia, we do not ask a penny from the British government to help us in training our officers. For fifty years back we have been taxing the Canadian people without asking a cent from the British government to aid us in military expenditure. Two militia Bills have been adopted for defraying the expenditure on behalf of the military defence of Canada ; time and again we were told that the expenditure was to be used for that purpose alone. But if you are going to take the pick of our young men, the best of our young officers that are trained in Kingston, and give them to Lord Lansdowne and .Mr. Chamberlain to serve the British government in Sierra Leone, or in the Transvaal, or in Rhodesia, with the prospect of becoming settlers in order to develop Cecil Rhodes' land in north Rhodesia, that he has not been able to settle with British people-
I say we are taxing the Canadian people I
upon false pretenses, and we are simply assisting the British government to play that little game under the flag of loyalty. I have nothing to say of what has taken place in the past. This motion has nothing to do with the South African question. The South African question might have come up if the correspondence askeu for by the other address had been brought down, i have asked for that correspondence during three months, and could not get it. But this correspondence has nothing to do with tire South African question. It has to do solely with the question of granting commissions to Canadian officers in the i>.,,isli army. I say that if we allow our young men to go into the British army, we should at least not offer them any inducements to do so at the expense of the Canadian people. When I say at the expense of the Canadian people I want to be understood. I do not say that we pay to send them there, that we pay them when they are there ; but I say we have paid for their education, we have voted a military budget every year to keep up our militia, and it is not right iliat an agent of the British government should be allowed to come here and take the pick of those young men in order to incorporate them in the British army. No doubt the British army should be improved ; I hope that Great Britain will recover her prestige that has been injured in South Africa. I cannot prevent the majority of this parliament, if they desire, from voting as much money as they like for sending contingents to South Africa : but they should tell the people of Canada frankly what is going on.
There is in that correspondence a long despatch from Lord Stratlicona to the government saying that he has done his best in order to have an increased number of commissions allowed to Canadian officers. 1 do not think it is the duty of the representative of Canada in England to say to the British government that the more of our young officers they take from us the (letter for Canada. As I said, I am willing to give every freedom to Canadian officers who want to serve in the British army ; but I do not think that our government should lend its assistance to offer them any inducement to do so. It is the duty of the government of Canada to provide for its military defence, but it is not the duty of the government of Canada to allow agents of the British Empire to come here and take away the best of our young officers to make settlers for their poor colonies.
Mr. MeCREARY. How would you prevent it ?

I say that the government of Canada should not become itself an agent of the British government for that purpose. Whether the government has done it or not, I cannot say. But Lord Minto has made these offers, Mr. Chamberlain has made these offers, as we find in these de-

spatches offering commissions in the West African police force with the understanding that it would become permanent employment, that the only leave of absence granted them would be from Africa to England and back, with no leave of absence to Canada. Mr. Speaker, I desire to say a word or two. I would say this, however, that we must remember we are a part of the British Empire, and it is the right of the sovereign in iny judgment to call upon all his subjects from one end of the empire to the other to respond to the invitation to defend their country in any way. It is no insult to the people of Canada, but on the contrary, it is a great compliment that her soldiers and officers should have so proved themselves in the late campaign that His Majesty's advisers are anxious to know whether they can obtain the services of Canadian officers. It is free and voluntary to any one who chooses to accept service in the Imperial army. It is the right of the sovereign of the empire and his advisers at all times to call upon those of his subjects who choose to accept that invitation. So. I say that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bourassaj very much mistakes the nature of the connection between this country and Great Britain if he thinks that the men who have gone from tItn Royal Military College to serve in the British army have not served Canada

"well by so doing. Sir, of these young men who, since that college was instituted, have been tendered commissions by the British government, we have every right to be proud, and it is pleasing to me to be able to remind the hon. gentleman behind me, that among them no men have distinguished themselves more than some of my fellow-countrymen of French origin. I beg further to remind him that of all the officers who have received distinctions for their conduct in the present campaign, the one who has received the highest distinction is a French Canadian, the son of one of the members of the Supreme Court bench, and I believe, I express the opinion of the overwhelming majority of my fellow-countrymen of French origin when 1 say that there will be found, I believe, no man but the hon. gentleman himself, who complains that the British government are seeking to obtain recruits from the ranks of our officers for service in defence of the empire in South Africa or elsewhere.

action which has been taken by the government in respect to this matter.

speechtext: I wish to put myself right in regard to this Bill. subtopic: MONTREAL AND SOUTHERN COUNTIES RAILWAY COMPANIES.
speechtext:
This Bill is of considerable importance. It has been brought down late in the session, and there is considerable doubt that the petition presented



to the House agrees with the main body of the Bill. I am inclined to think, notwithstanding what the chairman of the committee said, that this Bill is not in accordance with the petition presented to the House, and that it gives powers to this company that the House would not grant were we in possession of the facts. The Bill pretends to deal with certain matters affecting the electric railway and other railway systems in the city of Montreal. As a member of the Railway Committee, I must say that I am not at all aware what this Bill means, except that it involves principles which should not be passed without great consideration. We are now within twenty-four hours from prorogation, and I think the hon. gentleman should withdraw the Bill.

subtopic: MONTREAL AND SOUTHERN COUNTIES RAILWAY COMPANIES.
speechtext: I do not think the facts are as complicated as the hon. gentleman (Mr. McCreary) would suggest. There was a petition for an extension of the time to begin the line, and the petition was in absolute accordance with the notice given. In the Railway Committee, the company was given power to use steam, which it never prayed for in the petition, and it was also given power to extend its bonding privileges, which also was not asked in the petition. There was another clause giving power to cross the Victoria bridge at Montreal. That had not been mentioned in the notice, but that power rests with the company under the Railway Act. The main object of the Bill is to ask for an extension of time. The House, through one of its committees, has thought it proper to place in the Bill some provisions that were not prayed for, and it would not be fair, I think, to make the promoters of the Bill suffer for what was done by a committee of the House. If necessary, we can eliminate these powers that are objected to.

subtopic: MONTREAL AND SOUTHERN COUNTIES RAILWAY COMPANIES.
speechtext:
I quite agree with what the hon. member (Mr. Monk) has said and I really do not understand the opposition of some hon. members here. In order to meet the wishes of those opposed to the Bill, we will take out the objectionable clauses, and with that end in view, I beg to move, seconded by Mr. Davis :
That the following words be struck out (a) from the word ' by ' in the second line of section 1 to the word ' and ' in the third line inclusive ; (b) all the words at the end of subsection 2 of section 1, commencing with the words ' and for the ' In the seventeenth line thereof, to the end of the subsection ; (c) all the words of section 2.

Mr. McCreary.
It would be an injustice towards the promoters of the Bill to kill it in committee now.

Intercolonial Railway-To provide for payment of award of arbitrators in connection with Eastern Extension Railway, Nova Scotia, $671,836.

Judging from the discussion which took place in this House a few days ago, and in which this item was incidentally mentioned by some hon. gentlemen opposite, there seemed to be a little misconception as to the real nature of the appropriation which is now being asked from parliament; and, therefore, it will not be out of place to offer a few words of explanation as to the circumstances which have induced the government to place this item in the estimates. In the year 1877 the Intercolonial Railway had not reached the proportions it has to-day. It was confined to a single line of railway from Halifax to St. John and from Halifax to Rivi&re du Loup, and there was a branch from Truro to Pictou. The rest of the province of Nova Scotia was not

served by railway communication, and the people of that section of the country-the counties of Pictou, Antigonish, Guysborough, and the whole island of Cape Breton-petitioned and pressed upon the government-not only upon the Dominion government, but the provincial government-to have this railway extended at least from Nova Scotia to the Gulf of Canso.
The province of Nova Scotia was little able to undertake itself such a heavy task. It applied to the Dominion government for aid, and the Dominion government-at that time the government of Mr. Mackenize-in 1877, came to the conclusion that it would afford aid for the construction of a piece of road from New Glasgow to the Gulf of Canso, a distance of eighty miles. An Act was passed to that effect, and the aid which was then offered by the Dominion government was to give to any company which would undertake the construction of the eighty miles of road from New Glasgow to the Gulf of Canso, the piece of road which was then in existence, a part of the Intercolonial Kailway, from Truro to New Glasgow. An Act was passed to that effect in the session of 1877. Two years afterwards, when the government of Sir John Macdonald came into office, this arrangement wras ratified and an agreement entered into by the Dominion government, and provincial government and Cape Breton Railway and Coal Company. By that agreement, the Halifax and Cape Breton Railway and Coal Company undertook to build that section, which was known as the eastern extension from New Glasgow to the Gulf of Canso. The consideration which was given by the Dominion government consisted in the transfer in fee simple to that company of the section of the road between Truro and New Glasgow, the Dominion government, in the meantime, retaining that road in its possession until the other section between New Glasgow and the Gulf of Canso was thoroughly equipped and in operation. The government of Nova Scotia undertook at the same time to aid the enterprise of the Halifax and Cape Breton Railway and Coal Company in money. In the assistance which it gave, the Nova Scotia government disbursed actually a sum exceeding $670,000. It was stipulated then by that agreement-which is known in the correspondence as the tripartite agreement-that after the completion of the road by the company, which afterwards became the Eastern Extension Company, if that company failed to operate the road and equip it and build a ferry at the Gulf of Canso, then the ownership should be forfeited to the government.
Let me call the attention of the House to the fact that it was stipulated between the two parties that, in the event of the company failing to carry on the undertaking and operate the road, then its right in the road would be forfeited to the government. But, I want the House to understand that 1854
it was the government of Nova Scotia which was to become the owner of that valuable piece of road, should it be forfeited, and that government undertook to subsidize the company to the extent of $670,000 and more- in fact, to an extent exceeding $8,000 per mile. The road was built, and it became evident that the company could not operate it, and the company agreed to transfer the ownership to the province of Nova Scotia. The Dominion government, of course, consented, as had been agreed on the 1st of October, 1883, to the government of Nova Scotia taking possession of the road and operating it for its own benefit and advantage. Dp to that time all the agreement had been carried out except this, that the government of Canada was still in possession of the road between Truro and New Glasgow, but it was part of the agreement that on the 1st of October, 1883, when the province of Nova Scotia was to become proprietor in fee simple of that section of the road which had just been completed between New Glasgow and the Gulf of Canso, that province was to become also-under the terms of the agreement of 1877, ratified in 1879-proprietor absolutely of the section of road between Truro and New Glasgow. If that agreement had been carried out as stipulated, the province of Nova Scotia would have become owner and proprietor on the 1st of October, 1883, of the full extent of the road from Truro to the Gulf of Canso.
But on the 1st of October the government of Canada failed to comply with the conditions of the agreement, to which it had consented three or four years before ; and on the 20th of October, 1883, the government of Canada passed an order in council declaring its intention of complying with the agreement, but imposing on the province of Nova Scotia conditions which were not stipulated in the Act of 1879. The new conditions on which it declared itself ready to hand over the road to the Nova Scotia government were two. First, that Nova Scotia should not have control of the tariff, but that the tariff should be based on the tariff of the Intercolonial Railway. The second was that Nova Scotia should provide at once a stated amount of rolling stock, without any regard to the condition of the road. These conditions appear to have been imposed for the purpose of making it impossible for the government of Nova Scotia to acquire the railway, as was stipulated in 1877 and again in 1879.
The government of Nova Scotia could not comply with these conditions, and it had to abandon the vested right it had under the agreement, made some few years ago- in 1877 and 1879-between it and the Dominion government. The Nova Scotia government protested against the conditions imposed upon it by the government of Canada, protested against the government of Canada using its authority to prevent the Nova Scotia government from taking the

advantage which had accrued to it by the terms of the agreement under which it had paid the sum of $670,000. There is one point which I wish at once to press upon the attention of the House. The province of Nova Scotia at that time was not in the sound financial position in which it is today, and this undertaking was one, I may say, which was beyond the legitimate power of the province at that time-the aiding of such a road to the extent of $8,000 a mile. There have been many governments that have aided enterprises of this kind, but there has been no provincial government that has found it possible to aid a railway of that description to the extent of $8,000 a mile. And I can safely say that the province of Nova Scotia never would have dared to assume such a liability had it not been for the condition stipulated and ratified by two Acts of parliament, that, in the event of forfeiture, the ownership of the road would revert, not to the Dominion of Canada, but to the province of Nova Scotia. When the Dominion government practically took possession of the road in spite of the agreement it had with the government of Nova Scotia, I have no hesitation in characterizing its act as an absolute breach of faith. The government of Nova Scotia protested at the time, and it has kept on protesting ever since. When we came into power five years ago, we found that claim against the Dominion government still pending, though the government of Nova Scotia had pressed for recognition of its rights again and again. Its legitimate voice had never been heard and this unsettled claim was a sore rankling in the breast of the people of Nova Scotia. We thought it was not for the good government of Canada that such a claim should remain unsettled. So, we deemed it best, under the circumstances, to refer the claim to arbitrators for investigation and settlement upon the grounds of equity and justice. We selected as arbitrators gentlemen of the highest character. However we may differ as to the other conditions of that claim, there can be no doubt whatever as to the qualifications of the arbitrators. The first was Chief Justice Burton. I need but mention the name of Chief Justice Burton to make it unnecessary to qualify him. He is one of the most eminent jurists and the most conscientious and hhle judges that have adorned the bench of Ontario, which has been prolific of good men. The second arbitrator was a gentleman who has since become a member of this House, and who has attained quite a standing in it. I refer to our hon. colleague from Annapolis (Mr. Wade). The third arbitrator was Mr. Barbeau, one of the leading bankers of Montreal, a gentleman, perhaps, not well known to the members of this House, but well known in the city of Montreal; and none who know him will hesitate to give Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
him the highest qualification in his profession, not only as an eminent banker, but as a man of sterling honour and integrity. The arbitrators came to the conclusion that the province had suffered damages by the breach of contract on the part of the Dominion government, and was entitled to compensation. The only question in their minds was the amount of compensation to which the province was entitled. I may say, before going further, that the arbitrators did not hesitate to say that, in their opinion, the Dominion was absolutely warranted in its action in 1883, when it forced the province of Nova Scotia to forego the rights which had accrued to it through the bargain between the province and the Dominion. Let me, on this point read the views of the arbitrators :
But there is evidence which would warrant us in concluding that these conditions which were contained in the order in council of the 20 th October were not the true reasons for adopting the course then taken. A very short time previously, the Minister of Railways, when the province was about to raise funds to pay for the railway, gave the provincial authorities the most unqualified assurance that the Truro branch would be handed over, and yet we find the same minister, when the time had arrived for fulfilment of the promise, stating in parliament that the government had made up their minds that this road should not be disposed of. The true reason would rather seem to be that which was stated by the same Minister of Railways in his place in parliament, who, after referring to its vast importance to the coal mining industries and its important connection with the transport of coal and the coaling of steamers at the port of Halifax and from a variety of causes stated, it was found that it would be attended with great inconvenience and disadvantage, and that in fact parting with it would to a large extent dislocate the railway system as it had been carried on, and in another place he said it was the key of the Intercolonial situation, being the entrance to the coal fields, adding ' We have a splendid thing, and it would be absolutely impossible for us to give it away.'
So, the arbitrators found that the reason why the government of Canada did not carry out the contract it had made with the province by which the province would have become, and would to-day be, the owner of the road from Truro to the Gut of Canso, was that the government of Canada thought it better to keep the railway for themselves, and as it was put at the time- as they had a good thing in their hands they wanted to keep it. In the face of such a condition of things, is it not manifest that the province of Nova Scotia has been unfairly dealt with, and is entitled to compensation ? The province of Nova Scotia burdened itself with a loan in order to aid the construction of that railway. This she did in the full expectation that if the enterprise was not carried out by the company, and if forfeiture took place, the road would revert to the province, and the province would have this big asset of 120 miles of

railway between Truro and the Gut of Canso in one of the most important sections of the country. The government of Canada thought that instead of allowing the province of Nova Scotia to become the owner of that road it should keep the ownership for itslf. So, the arbitrators have come to the conclusion that the province is entitled to fair compensation, and it finds that that fair compensation is the amount they contributed to the road, that is, $071,000. These being the facts, it seems to me that the government of Canada is only fulfilling its duty in doing now what should have been done eighteen years ago. No. I should not say that, for we cannot do what should have been done eighteen years ago. There is no question before us now of the province of Nova Scotia becoming the owner of that road. But it is only fair that we should repair the mischief that has been done so far as lies in our power, and should compensate the province of Nova Scotia for the expenditure it made at that time, of the benefits of which it was deprived.
Some days ago, I heard my hon. _friend from South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) make the observation: When is there to be an end of this bringing of claims by the provinces against the Dominion ?	1 have no hesitation in saying that if we make contracts as has been done in this case with a province, and claims arise out of those contracts, those claims must be adjusted. If the Dominion government had not entered into a contract with the government of the province of Nova Scotia, there would have been no claims. But the Dominion government went out of its way to make a contract with the province; a claim has arisen out of that. Shall we say that this claim shall not be recognized ? Why should it not be recognized ? Why should a government be more exempt from liability than an individual ? Is there any law, human or divine, why a government should not be responsible for its laches ? I submit to the sense of fairness and justice in the breast of every man, that the government cannot, under such circumstances, say that there is no legal claim. Sometimes another thing has been done, sometimes a claim has been ignored, or it has been settled according to the views of the Dominion government, without regard to the views of the local government. Whenever there are claims of that kind, if you wish for a settlement which will be final, or, as Mr. Blake said, ' finally final,' the only way to get it is to have a compromise between the parties by a judicial arbitration. Take the case of Prince Edward Island, which was disposed of a few days ago. That claim is settled now for ever, you will never hear of it any more. My hon. friend shakes his head-I will give him the reason why I say so. A claim was presented by Prince Edward Island against
the Dominion government about fifteen years ago. In 1885, the Dominion government, having ignored the claim, Prince Edward Island carried its complaint to the foot of the Throne, to the Imperial authorities. The Imperial authorities referred it to the Canadian government, with an intimation that the claim ought to be settled. That claim has been pending ever since, but, we have now settled it, and the settlement will be ' finally final,' because we have made an agreement with the province of Prince Edward Island under which they will accept the sum that we have given them as a full settlement of the claim, and they have given us a quit claim, and have placed it on record in their legislation.
The right hon. gentleman was told by two representatives from Prince Edward Island that it was not a settlement.

I was told on the floor of the House, by two gentlemen who represent Prince Edward Island, that, in their view, the amount of money paid is not sufficient. But, while those two gentlemen from Prince Edward Island have told us that the amount is not sufficient, the legislature of Prince Edward Island has solemnly passed an Act whereby they discharge us of any further claim upon this ground. Nothing could be more final than this, you have an Act of the legislature itself.
Does the hon. gentleman refer to the future as well as the present ? Does that cover all claims for the future ?
It covers all the claims which have arisen out of the nonfulfilment of the terms of union.
Past, present and future ?

Well, I fear I cannot answer my hon. friend as to that. If my hon. friend is going to look to the future, I am afraid there is no tribunal in the world that could satisfy him ; I will refer him to the day of judgment for that. But, I mean to say for the past, and up to this year 1901, all the claims Prince Edward Island had against this government arising out of the nonfulfilment of the terms of union, have been settled, and the settlement has been sanctioned by the legislature of Prince Edward Island. In the same way In this case. I wish to say to my hon. friend from Lanark (Mr. Haggart), that this claim for which we now ask an appropriation, will be absolutely settled, settled for ever, because the province of Nova Scotia has agreed with us to refer the claim to arbitration, and evidently, when two parties go to arbitration the award is a final settle-

ment of the claim. When the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) was speaking of the claims of Manitoba with reference to the Canadian Pacific Railway, and wnen he said that every year a new settlement had to be made, there was a reason for it, because the government of that day never took the precaution to have a judicial arbitration or to have an Act of parliament. But, here we have taken the precaution to have a judicial arbitration. The province of Nova Scotia has agreed to refer this claim to three arbitrators, the award has been pronounced, and when the money is paid the claim will be for ever settled.

I think there is one fact which has not been mentioned. The government of Nova Scotia was a consenting party to the transfor of this portion of the road from New Glasgow to the Gut of Canso. and made as a condition an extension of the road in Cape Breton.

The government of Nova Scotia never was a willing party to anything of the kind. She was forced to give her consent, she was powerless in the hands of the Dominion government, and only accepted under protest that arrangement, asserting that she had been deprived of the rights which had accrued under the contract ratified in 1879. I submit to the committee that it is not conducive to the welfare of the Dominion that there should exist claims of that kind against the Federal government on the part (of any of the provinces. We want every province to feel that it has received the justice to which it is entitled. On that ground I ask parliament to vote this money for the settlement of that long pending claim. I am satisfied that the committee, at all events a majority of it. will come to the conclusion that it was a wise action on the part of this government to settle the claim in this manner.

The right hon. gentleman has stated his case very clearly. According to my remembrance, I had some communication with the Nova Scotia government in reference to this particular claim, and I remember submitting it to the Minister of Justice, who had been premier of the province, Sir John Thompson. It is true, as the right hon. gentleman says, that we were in possession of a line of road from Truro to New Glasgow, and that the Nova Scotia government were very anxious to extend that road from New Glasgow to the Gut of Canso. offering to furnish a ferry to cross the Gut. They made arrangements with some company to secure the building of that road, giving them some assistance to extend it. I believe they expended over $670,000. There was a tripartite agreement entered into between the railway company which was constructing that road, the Dominion government, Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
and the Nova Scotia government, under which agreement the Dominion government were to give over to the Nova Scotia government this section of the road after it was built, and upon certain fixed terms. The Dominion government properly made it a condition, before handing the road over to the Nova Scotia government, that the latter should have material enough to work that branch, because it was essential, not only in the interest of the Dominion, but of the province of Nova Scotia, that the line from Truro to New Glasgow should be efficiently worked, and that from New Glasgow to the Gut of Canso should be efficiently worked ; and the Dominion government' retained, as they ought to retain, the right to approve of the tariffs to be charged over that road. That is a peculiar right which is vested in the Dominion.

Does the hon. gentleman mean to say that if the local legislature gives a charter to a company and the company runs a road, that the Dominion government has a right to say what the tariff will be, and not the local government ?
That was the agreement with them.
That is what the Dominion government wanted to do.

That was a part of the agreement when the Dominion handed over to the local legislature the road from New Glasgow to the Gut of Canso. The fact of the matter Is, that the Nova Scotia government were not in a position to put rolling stock upon the road. They had expended the whole of the credit of the province in getting the part from New Glasgow to the Gut of Canso constructed. It was a valuable asset to them. If they had been compelled to run the road, not only would they have lost the amount of money which was requisite to put rolling stock on the road, but. they would have been subjected to a continuous loss in working the whole road. That was the position of the province at that time. It was a worthless asset to the province, and. as I understood him, the right hon. leader of the government said that there is no correspondence in the direction which I state. I have a recollection that there was some correspondence between the Nova Scotia government and the Dominion government 'at that time on the point of their taking over this particular portion of the road and building a ferry at the Gut of Canso, and on the promise of the extension of the road through Cape Breton to Sydney, the Nova Scotia government would very willingly vest their claims in this particular undertaking in the Dominion government.
Did the government assent to that ?
I think they did, and I think they performed that part of the agreement with the province ?
They refused to.

That is a subject to which I drew the attention of the right hon. gentleman, and which he carefully avoided, and which I do not think has been presented to the arbitrators. Now, the hon. Minister of Finance, in defending this arbitration the other day, stated that he had followed the lines exactly that were followed in the settlement between Ontario and Quebec and the Dominion government. I cannot understand the similitude. The hon. gentleman must remember that the whole matter was explained in parliament and that parliament was asked to give authority to the executive to give to these arbitrators the right to go past the legality of the transaction and to inquire into the equities of the case at that time between Ontario and Quebec and the Dominion. What were the facts of the matter ? In that arbitration between Ontario, Quebec and the Dominion, there was to be taken into consideration the interest on a certain sum that had been due from the old province of Canada to the province of Ontario. The interest on that amount was retained from the subsidies due to the different provinces. That amount was afterwards assumed, under the Act of 1884, by the Dominion government, and in order to return to the different provinces the amount of money to which they were entitled in the form of interest which had been deducted from the subsidies, the claims of the two provinces had to be decided. The equities were on all sides, with the Dominion, and with the provinces, but in this case the equities were entirely upon one side, on the side of the province of Nova Scotia. The difference between the plan adopted by us and the plan adopted by hon. gentlemen opposite is this : We heard nothing of this claim being settled. The hon. gentlemen opposite took it upon themselves by order in council to frame regulations under which this case was submitted to the arbitrators. As to the legality of the claim of Nova Scotia there is no doubt whatever that there is no legal claim. The right hon. leader of the government must know that, because he has the evidence of it in the Department of Justice. The case was submitted to the late Sir John Thompson and to different Ministers of Justice, and they advised the department over which I had the honour to preside, the Department of Railways and Canals, that Nova Scotia had no legal claim. Having no legal claim, the duty of the government was to come and explain the facts of the case to parliament, and get an Act of this parliament for the purpose of submitting the equities to a court to decide upon them. The hon. gentleman says that there will be no finality, and that
I was arguing that when a province has a claim against the Dominion it should not be entertained. I did not make any such argument as that, but my argument was that the claims of the provinces, having been settled from time to time by different subsidy Acts, you have no right to go past these Acts for "the purpose of fishing up what may or not be a claim against the Dominion government. In the Prince Edward Island case, the first subsidy Act was revived by an Act of 1873, and it was revived again by an Act of 1884, by which there was a general settlement of the subsidies to which the different provinces were entitled. By a special Act afterwards, Prince Edward Island was given $20,000 per year, which was added to the subsidy to be given to that province. My argument was this : Is it not probable, is it not likely, that all the claims of the different provinces were settled up to the time that the increased subsidies were granted ? What I stated was that where there has been an increased subsidy from time to time given to the different provinces and where the amount to which they are entitled has been fixed by a subsidy Act, these claims, which existed for years before that subsidy Act was passed, were wiped out by the sub-isidy Act. I admit that a claim through a contract might occur between the Dominion government and the province after the subsidy Act had been passed, which might entitle the province to claim against the Dominion government, and that it might be submitted to arbitration for the purpose of deciding upon it. But, first of all, I think authority should be obtained from this parliament to submit the case to the arbitrators. The distinction, then, that I draw between the course which has been pursued by the hon. Minister of Finance in this case and the course we adopted in 1883, as to the settlement of the claims between Ontario, Quebec and the Dominion, is such as to demonstrate that there is no parallel whatever. In this case, in regard to the legality of the claim, there is no doubt about it that we are not entitled to give the province of Nova Scotia anything. I may be mistaken in the statement I make, but I believe that the province of Nova Scotia was a consenting party when the Dominion of Canada acquired possession of that particular section of the road, and that the conditions were that they should operate the road and work the ferry across the Gut of Canso and build the road through Cape Breton to Sydney.

This is one of the questions that the House in committee must naturally shut their eyes to. The committee must vote blindly on a question that they had little time at their disposal to unravel, and they must rely mainly on the statements that are made by those who take the responsibility of introducing this measure. Any one w'ho has taken the trouble to inquire into it must have been greatly amused at the light in which the right hon. leader of the
I

government (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) placed the case. The right hon. gentleman stated as one ground for the claim that the Dominion government had practically with force taken possession of the road. I took down the right hon. gentleman's words and X do not wish to torture them into any other meaning, because if the right hon. gentleman intended to convey that meaning, it is very important indeed.
I stand by what I said.
I have no doubt that the right hon. gentleman has relied mainly upon the award rather than upon having looked carefully into the evidence itself.

I will give my authority. My authority is the hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart). I stated that while the government of Canada should have handed over the road to the province of Nova Scotia on the 1st of October, 1883, they passed an order in council on the 20th of that month, stating that they were ready to hand over this piece of road to the province of Nova Scotia on the condition that the province would equip the road with a certain amount of rolling stock. My hon. friend from Lanark stated a moment ago that this exhausted the credit of Nova Scotia, and that it was not in a position to equip the road in the manner forced upon it by the government of Canada.

That explanation modifies the statement previously made by the Prime Minister, to the effect that the Dominion government forced Nova Scotia into that position knowing at the time that Nova Scotia was financially embarrassed. I was not aware that it was the duty of the Dominion government to be guided by the financial position of a province, but I have to say that Nova Scotia never wanted that road for the reason that the province was financially embarrassed. The Dominion government imposed the rates and the province said that these rates were too low, and that under them they could not make the road pay. The answer of the miners of Nova Scotia was that it was a question whether there should be high rates, or whether the coal should be carried at sufficiently low rates to develop the mines, so that the money might go into the pockets of the people, rather than that the high rates should go into the provincial treasury. It is quite true that the pretense was set up at one time that Nova Scotia did require the road, but in 1884 when the Prime Minister of the province was justifying the action of the government of which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding) was a distinguished member, this is what the Hon. Mr. Pipes had to say with regard to the bargain made with the Dominion government:

It will be remembered that when I was in Ottawa in December of 1882, I offered the Dominion government this railway if they would pay the Allan Company's outlay, take over the Eastern Extension, and give the province the right within two years of taking the roads hack upon paying the Dominion government the amount they would be called upon to pay the Allan Company. That proposition was not accepted. When I made it I thought that two years would give the people of this province a full opportunity of considering the advantages of having their roads operated _ by the Dominion government, and In that time it would be found to be a policy so advantageous to the province that the legislature would not be willing to take the roads out of the hands of the government.
His contention was that if they could have induced the Dominion government to take hold of the road, to pay the Halifax and Cape Breton Coal Company their outlay, and to operate the road for two years, the people of Nova Scotia would have been thoroughly convinced that it was in the best interests of the province that the road should remain in the hands of the Dominion government. It had been said that the Dominion government had forced a hard bargain, that the province was compelled to yield, and that the exhorbitant demands made by the Dominion government both as to the additional rolling stock and as to the rates, might end in a legal contest. But this is what the present Minister of Finance, speaking in the Nova Scotia legislature, had to say on that point:
But. suppose the government had succeeded, there were victories which were worse than defeat, and when he looked carefully into the figures connected with the matter, he was Inclined to question whether success in a contest with the Dominion government might not have been more disastrous than failure.
In other words, if the province succeeded in the courts, the victory over the Dominion would be more disastrous than if the province failed.
Taking the cost of the road and the amount to be expended in repairs at $1,500,000. that would have involved an annual charge of $75,000. Mr. Scott said that with a fair tariff the government could realize $60,000 from the branch and $10,000 from Eastern Extension. Suppose that the government had done better than this and made $75,000. In that case, they would have made both ends meet, but what gain would it have been to the people of Cape Breton or Yarmouth or Digby for the government to go on with an enterprise which at the utmost would only have paid annual interest, and when the rates could not be increased without Imposing taxation on the people of Colchester, Pictou and Antigonish, and seriously affecting the coal trade? That being the case, they thought it better to come to an arrangement with the Dominion government. He (Hon. Mr. Fielding) was not willing to fight when he saw there was nothing to fight for. The estimates in regard to the value of the Pictou branch were made at a time when people were disposed to take a rose-coloured view of things. For himself, he had never entertained a high opinion

of the calculations, especially as they were prepared in the interests of the syndicate. He thought it best, therefore, to get rid of the property in such a way as to leave the province free from loss. Everything that the government could have accomplished by the policy of taking over the road had been accomplished by the policy before the House without any of the disadvantages of the former policy.
Can language he plainer than that ? The Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) plainly announced that it would have been idle to have gone into the courts to contest with the Dominion government as to whether they'were taking a proper course with regard to the rates or to the rolling stock, because, as he told the people he so ably represented in the legislature, if they succeeded in a suit of that kind it would be disastrous to the province. The hon. gentleman states that the road would no more than pay its expenses with the advanced rates. The hon. gentleman states that even under circumstances of that kind, if the public purse were served, the people would have to suffer correspondingly ; and that therefore everything that could be accomplished by taking the road over from the Dominion government was accomplished by the settlement made with the Dominion government. But another distinguished gentleman had something to say on the subject in the Nova Scotia legislature, that was Mr. Dongley, at present, I believe, the Attorney General of the province. This is what he had to say during the same debate :
Hon. gentlemen opposite had charged the Dominion government with forcing this province to accept this bargain, as if that was anything to boast of. But he was going to show that this government was not forced into the bargain. He stated boldly that he believed that if at any stage the Dominion government had offered to give the local government the branch on their own terms, he believed this government would have subserved the interests of Nova Scotia by handing over the two roads on the same terms on which they did hand them over. But Mr. Longley went further. He said :
Instead of this bargain being forced upon them by the Dominion government, it was forced upon the Dominion government by the local government, who placed the whole subject before them in so clear a light that they dared not impose upon us. Hon. gentlemen might smile, but he said they forced upon the Dominion government a bargain which had been proved to be advantageous to the interest of Nova Scotia.
Mr. Longley. the present Attorney General of the province of Nova Scotia, was one of the eminent counsel employed at the arbitration. But another gentleman of high standing in the province of Nova Scotia made a speech since this award was made -Mr. E. M. Macdonald, whom I imagine the hon. Minister of Finance knows very well. This award was made on the 19th of July, 1900, and Mr. Macdonald, who was also one of the counsel on behalf of Nova Scotia, made a speech in the legislature on the 26th of March, 1901, in which he said :
While this transfer was inadequate as regarded compensation, yet it had one important advantage to the province. It was l-ecognized that those who justified the transfer on the ground that it was more >in the interest of the province of Nova Scotia that the Dominion government should control this railway, spoke correctly and that they laid down a policy that history had justified.
Now, we have in a nutshell the attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite. I think I might well sit down after calling as witnesses these gentlemen whom I have quoted. I have pointed out that a distinguished member of the legislature, who was engaged as counsel before the arbitrators, has declared that the policy which was pursued in 1881 by the province of Nova Scotia was a wise policy, and the best thing that could be done. We have Mr. Longley declaring that the Dominion government had not forced the province, but that the province had forced the Dominion government. We have the Minister of Finance contending that nothing was contended for, but that everything that could be obtained for the road was more than obtained if the Dominion took over the road. I challenge the Minister of Finance, who is well acquainted with the subject, to say that Nova Scotia has sustained a loss. If Nova Scotia has not sustained a loss, where is the claim ? There is absolutely no claim. Nova Scotia has no more right to come in and make that claim for the sums which were paid by the legislature towards the construction of that road than the province of Ontario has to claim from the Dominion seven or eight million dollars which have been granted by the local legislature to railways in that province. No hon. member of this House will pretend to draw a distinction in favour of any province because it granted a subsidy to a road which became part of the Intercolonial. If there were any reason why subsidies should be returned to a province, there would be the greater reason where the subsidies were granted to roads which are not government roads, and why ? For the simple reason that the Intercolonial is maintained entirely out of the public purse, while the provinces and municipalities have struggled to give subsidies to railways from one end of Canada to the other.
I have scanned hurriedly the aid that has been given to railways by the Dominion government, and I am sure it will be instructive to the House to see how it stands at the present time. The whole sum that has been given appears to be in round numbers $150,000,000. Of that sum $56,000,000 was given to the great trunk line, the Canadian Pacific, and $60,000,000 to the Intercolonial : and the total sum given to all other railways in Canada amounts to only $33,000,000 or $34,000,000. In other words, the Intercolonial Railway has had spent on capital account nearly twice as much as all

the other railways in Canada, excluding the Canadian Pacific Railway, which is a road that concerns all Canada. Ndw, Sir, what state of things is that ? The Intercolonial Railway was built mainly in the interest of the maritme provinces, and they have derived most of the benefits of that road. The Dominion ti*feasury has been taxed and bled, and it has a right to be taxed and bled, because the Dominion made that bargain and should live up to it faithfully, no matter what the cost may be. It is too late in the day now to attempt to repudiate it; but I ask if it is fair for the province of Nova Scotia time and again, whenever it suits it, to come here and make a claim on so flimsy a ground. I ask hon. gentlemen from the province of Quebec: Are you going to claim the $300,000 that was given by your province on precisely the same terms to the Drummond County Railway? Are the people of Ontario going to make claims of a similar kind ?
We are told to-night that this has legislative sanction in Nova Scotia. But that does not mean anything. It means simply that the legislature of Nova Scotia will be bound by its sanction so long as it does not feel disposed to put forth a new claim. What we desire above all things, and what I am sure the Minister of Finance would like to see, is finality. The Finance Minister was one of the contending parties in the Nova Scotia legislature. He took an important part in the negotiations and he accepted the sum then paid over to the province, which covered every outlay of the province in the matter. That was paid and that should have put an end to all demands. Why did he not stand by the bargain they agreed to ? What followed ? The hon. gentleman submitted himself to be dragged in as a witness in a case against the Dominion treasury of which he is the custodian. There has not been any evidence produced to show that the province sustained any loss. If it could be shown that by reason of the action of the Dominion government, Nova Scotia had sustained a loss, we could understand her advancing a claim to be recouped, but there is absolutely no claim made on that ground. With regard to the arbitrators, no one questions their respectability, but there are no judges or arbitrators so respectable that their judgments may not be appealed from. And this is an appeal to parliament not to sustain a decision that is destitute of every feature which would warrant the payment of a cent. As my hon. friend from South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) has very well asked : Where are we going to stop ? Why, the province of Ontario, on just as sound a basis, might come forward to-morrow and claim the subsidies paid by that province, amounting to $7,000,000, and the bonuses given by Ontario municipalities amounting to some $9,000,000, from this government. We are now asked to pay $670,000 for the principal, and later on we will have a demand for the Mr. CLANCY.
interest ; and because we passed an Act in 1882 declaring that all railways, under certain conditions, were for the general advantage of Canada, -we will have a raid on the Dominion treasury by the provinces to be recouped for the subsidies they gave these railways. I have no hesitation in saying that this claim has not a redeeming feature in it. From start to finish, the province of Nova Scotia has never claimed that it sustained a loss. We may well despair of the future of this country when we find that it is not possible to make a bargain with any province which that province will stand by.

I can see absolutely no analogy between the position of Nova Scotia and these arbitrators and the ease of any other province arising out of subsidies given to enterprises which were subsequently declared for the general advantage of Canada. Let me briefly state the facts which gave rise to this arbitration, so that we may understand what the difficulty was. When the House understands the facts involved and is not led away by side issues, which have no bearing on the question in hand, hon. members will see that the claim submitted to the arbitrators was a perfectly legitimate one. In 1874, and some years previous, there existed in Nova Scotia' a line of railway extending from Truro to Pictou. On the 19th May, 1874, a resolution was passed in the House of Commons declaring the railway from Truro to Pictou to be under the control of the Dominion government.
Does the hon. gentlemau meau that the Dominion government had issued a charter ?

The Dominion government owned the road. The railway came into existence previous to confederation. This particular branch was the property of the Dominion government. In 1874 a resolution was passed in this House which reads :
That the government be authorized to negotiate, during the parliamentary recess, for the transfer of the railway from Truro to Pictou to some organized company, on condition that such company will extend the said railway from New Glasgow or Pictou to the Gulf of Cans'), or some place in Cape Breton, within a specified time, and such transfer be subject to the approval of parliament at the next session.
What does that mean ? It means that in order to induce a company to construct a railway from New Glasgow to Port Mulberry, in the Gulf of Canso, the Dominion parliament undertook to transfer its branch from Truro to Pictou to the new company. Not only was that resolution passed at that time, but subsequently the province of Nova Scotia, interested in the construction of this piece of road from New Glasgow to the port of Mulgrave, entered into a contract with a man named Abbott, who, at

that time, was acting for the Halifax and Cape Breton Railway and Coal Company, for the construction of this road. That contract was entered into on the 31st October, 1876. And, in 1877, the matter came before this House, and, by statute, 40 Victoria chapter 46, the contract entered into between the province of Nova Scotia and this company was ratified by this parliament. By the Act passed at that time, it provided :
The Pictou and Truro Branch Railway, including sufficient land for the purposes thereof, and the stations and buildings thereon necessary for the use of the railway, but without any of the rolling stock, shall be transfered absolutely to the person or the company constructing the fine from New Glasgow to the Strait of Canso, and providing a proper steam ferry across the strait, as soon as such railway is constructed, with proper rolling stock and other appurtenances, and such ferry provided to the satisfaction of the Minister of Public Works.
Is that authority for a transfer or does that confirm a transfer ?

It confirms an agreement entered into between the province of Ontario and this ''company to construct this road from New Glasgow to Port Mulgrave. The Dominion government becomes a party to that contract, because it undertakes to say to the contractor : If you will fulfil your obligation to the province of Nova Scotia and construct this road, we will transfer to you the line from Truro to Pictou. The contract proceeded. And then, in 1879, we have another step in the proceedings, a step to which the Dominion government becomes a party. And I would point out to my hon. friend from Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) that there is no comparison between this case and the case to which he refers. This is a case that must stand on its own merits ; it is a distinct case of breach of agreement on the part of the Dominion government. On the 1st of February, 1879, a tripartite agreement was entered into. The Dominion government, the provincial government, and the railway I have first spoken about are the parties. And by this agreement it is provided that the contractors are to build what now becomes the Eastern Extension Railway, and it constitutes an obligation of the Dominion as to the transfer, and by which it was provided that the Truro branch should be retained by the Dominion government until the Eastern Extension Railway ito the Gut of Canso and the steam ferry across the strait should be completed, equipped and established, in accordance with the existing contract or any modification thereof that might be agreed to by the company and the Nova Scotia government, to the satisfaction of the Nova Scotia government, and that upon such completion the absolute right of property in the said Pictou branch should be conveyed to the company on certain terms. Now, the terms were fixed at that time by the solemn agreement
then entered into. Thus, the Dominion government was bound, on the performance by the contractor of certain conditions, to transfer this Pictou branch to him. Things 'went on from 1879 to 1882. In 1882, the contractor, not proceeding with the work as he should have done, it was found necessary by the Nova Scotia government to draw the attention of the Dominion government, the other party to the agreement, to the unsatisfactory progress made by the contractor. As a result of the representation made by the Nova Scotia government, the matter was referred to the then Minister of Public Works, and it comes before him. The parties were heard ; the delay for finishing the road was extended from 1st of March, 1882, to 1st of October, 1883. That delay expiring on the 1st of October, 1883, it was within the power of the Nova Scotia government, upon recouping to the Eastern Extension Railway a certain amount that they had been obliged to spend, to enter into possession of the Eastern Extension Railway and the Pictou branch.
Upon what condition ?

Under the conditions fixed in the tripartite agreement. The conditions were, that if the contractors did not carry out their agreement by 1st of October, 1883, then the Nova Scotia government entered into possession of the road, the Eastern Extension Railway, and entering into possession of the Eastern Extension branch, they became entitled to possession of the Truro-Pictou branch.
But only when they had complied with certain conditions ?
Complied with the conditions settled with the contractor.
No other conditions ?

My hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) has never read the contract. The delay expired on 1st of October, 1883. The Nova Scotia government took the steps necessary to pay the contractor for the Eastern Extension, so that they might be entitled to get possession of that portion of the road. It then remained to decide how far they might get possession of the Truro-Pictou branch, which was still in the possession of the Dominion government. But, the Dominion government say to the Nova Scotia government: It is all right; get possession of the Eastern Extension-the Dominion government could not prevent that, because it was a local concern under a local charter. If they had done that and entered into possession of the Eastern Extension they would have had a railway that began nowhere and ended nowhere-began at New Glasgow and went on to Port Mulgrave.
Does my hon. friend (Mr. Fitzpatrick) say New Glasgow is nowhere ?
From a railway standpoint.
Did the province enter into possession of the road ?

If my hou. friend will permit me to go on, I will explain. The Federal government said to the' local government : Take the Eastern Extension. And the local government did take it. But, the provincial government said : Comply with the rest of the bargain, and give us the rest of the extension from Truro to Pictou. They delayed until the 20th of the month, and then they said : We will give you the Truro and Pictou branch. But, they provided the terms and conditions under which the transfer was to be made. But the terms under which that transfer should have been made were fixed by the tripartite agreement of February 18th, 1879, and they ought to have left it to that agreement, and they ought to have handed over the road on those terms.

The province took over the road and received the Pictou branch, on condition that they were to operate it efficiently as stated there, and that the rolling stock were to be put on, and the tariff should be the tariff of the Intercolonial Railway.

I will read the conditions, and the hon. gentleman will see how near it is to the statement he has made :
That the company, after the completion of the road, should efficiently and continuously operate both lines to the satisfaction of the Lieutenant Governor at a fair and reasonable tariff of charges, which should be made and established by the company, subject to the approval of the government of Nova Scotia, and which should be only altered or amended with the assent and approval of that government, and any difference of opinion as to any item of such tariff should be submitted to the Minister of Public Works of the Dominion as a referee, whose decision should be final and binding.
Hear, hear.

I am afraid my hon. friend does not understand the point I am making. This was done under the agreement of 1879, but when, in 1883, the province asked to have the road handed over, the Dominion government changed the conditions so as to provide for the fixing of the rates by the Federal government and not by the local government, and also that the equipment should be such as was decided by the Federal government Now, I am not going to ask the House to take my construction of this modification of the lagreement. I am going to ask the House to take the construction put upon that modification by the arbitrators, from a legal Mr. FITZPATRICK.
standpoint. Here is what the arbitrators say, dealing with the order in council of October 20th :
It treats the road and ferry as not having been built, it then imposes two conditions which we have no hesitation in saying were unwarranted under the Act of parliament, and wholly illegal.
Now, the House may decide on this question of law between the opinion of the Chief Justice and the opinion of my hon. friend from Bothwell. That is the position of affairs at that time. The Federal government at that time used such duress with respect to the province of Nova Scotia, they placed that province in such a position that it was impossible for it to do otherwise, unless it was willing to have the whole road they had endeavoured to get constructed, obliged to submit to the terms they had imposed upon it.	,
I am afraid the hon. gentleman is casting a serious doubt on the veracity of the respectable gentleman -who contended the other way in the province of Nova Scotia.

It is not on the veracity of the hon. gentleman I reflect at all, it is upon the construction put by my hon. friend upon what he said. 1 beg to differ with him. I do not want to take my construction from my hon. friend, however adroit he may be in some things ; and I am not called upon to discuss the question of the veracity of the Minister of Finance, because he having testified there is no man in this country who will doubf his veracity.
