Now, the position was at this time that the province of Nova Scotia had expended, in connection with the construction of the Eastern Extension road, a very large sum, and the Dominion government, notwithstanding the solemn contract they had entered into to hand over this road as a consideration to induce the Nova Scotia government to make this expenditure, when they have them in a hole, and when they find that Nova Scotia is saddled with this enormous liability, they say to them : Keep that Eastern Extension and do as you please with your portion of the road, or give it to us and we will give you $1,200,000, over $700,000 less than had been expended upon it. Under these circumstances Nova Scotia submitted, and from that day to this Nova Scotia has continued protesting against the bargain. Finally the matter was referred to arbitrators to determine, not as to whether Nova Scotia was entitled to receive back the subsidies given to a railway built within its borders, but as to whether Nova Scotia, having been induced to enter this agreement on representations made by the Dominion government, which representations were afterwards repudiated by the government-whether in good faith and justice the Dominion government ought to carry out its agreement. That was the question submitted to the arbitra-

tors, and that is the question upon which the arbitrators unanimously found for Nova Scotia. That is the case.
There is one observation I would like to make with regard to this. What does the Solicitor General think about the proper measure of damages for such a breach of contract ?
The measure of damages has been settled by the arbitrators, and I beg to refer to their better opinion on the subject.

I thought probably my hon. friend would give me some such answer as that. There is one matter in connection with this arbitration that 1 do not quite follow. I may say that looking at the award as a whole, it does not seem in some cases to be expressed in very lucid terms. In saying that I do not in the' slightest degree desire to reflect upon Sir George Burpee, because I do not think it was drafted by him. I have perused many judgments of that very eminent jurist, and I have found them characterized by a clearness and lucidity which are not always present in this award. I do not understand from the terms of this award why it is that interest has been refused the province of Nova Scotia. The way in which that is dealt with in the award is this :
As to the interest claimed, there are many reasons why it should not, in our opinion, be allowed. It was not claimed for many years, and although claims were made by the province from time to time, they were made on different grounds, for altogether different matters, or, as is sometimes said, for better terms. The present arrangement having resulted favourably in a proper working of the road, benefiting the province as well as the Dominion, we think the ends of justice will be satisfied by refusing the claim for interest.
Well, I am bound to say that I do not see very much in these observations of the arbitrators that would prevent Nova Scotia from ' coming back at some future time and claiming interest. The province has to be congratulated upon that, because, of course, if a new reference were made in the same terms in which this is couched, It is perfectly open to the province at some future time to claim that interest. The reference has been made under these terms :
The arbitrators in making their award shall not be bound to decide according to the strict rules of law or evidence, but may decide upon equitable principles.
A subsequent claim with regard to interest if referred to arbitration in the same terms, leaves that question perfectly open to the province. I maintain that is the case.
The reference is couched in the same language as is used in connection with the interprovincial arbitration.

I am not finding any fault with the terms of the reference.
I may say, as my hon. friend has referred to it, that I do not think the two cases are at all parallel in that respect. In that case there were claims on both sides, and, therefore, it might be fair under an Act of parliament to couch the reference in the terms referred to. I do not say that is unfair now, I am only observing, in reply to what my hon. friend has said, that I do not think the cases are parallel. My object in making these remarks was to point out that apparently the province has suffered an injustice in this respect by not receiving interest, as I see nothing in the reasons of the arbitrators to justify a denial of interest, assuming the claim is valid. I suppose the province will see that that is done.
There is one other observation to make. I would like to know from the right hon. gentleman who has presented this matter to the House, whether he does not think that the claims of the municipalities referred to in this award are just as deserving as the claim which has been made by the province. It is>
true that the arbitrators in dealing with this matter did not take into consideration the claims of these municipalities, but the reason they did not do so was the fact that the terms of reference excluded the consideration of those claims. Now, so far as I understand the basis on which this award is made up, there is only one basis on which the arbitrators proceeded to consider the question of damages.	That was the point concerning
which I asked my hon. friend, the Solicitor General, a question, which he thought it better not to answer, and I excuse him under the circumstances for not making any ijeply other than he did. It is clear the arbitrators in dealing with this claim based their award upon the amount of subsidies the province had paid. It is perfectly clear that the award does not show that any damages were sustained by reason of the alleged breach of contract. Therefore, if the arbitrators, having dealt with this claim on the basis of the amount of subsidy paid to the railways, it follows irresistibly, it seems to me, that the municipalities which have granted aid to this railway are just as much entitled to have their claims passed upon in the same way as the province. I would like my hon. friend to state to the House what his view is in regard to that. I am not discussing at present the question as to whether this claim should have been /referred or not. I think the claim, having been referred to these arbitrators, and the province of Nova Scotia having entered into an agreement for that puipose, the only thing for parliament to do is to vote the amount of this award, but if this is a right principle upon which to proceed, in so far as the province of Nova Scotia is concerned, I hold that it is a right principle upon which to proceed as far as the various municipalities are concerned. I can see no distinction between the two cases.

I would like to Inquire of the hon. gentleman whether he does not think that the fact that a contract, even though not actually the subject of legislation, hut a legislative contract, having been entered into between the government of Nova Scotia and the government of Canada, it would distinguish the case entirely from that of the municipalities which may have given aid to this road, and with which the Dominion government had no contract ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I observed, and in this I understand the hon. Solicitor General to concur, that it was perfectly plain In this case that so far as the amount of damages which have been awarded by the arbitrators was concerned, it was determined solely by the consideration that a certain amount of subsidy had been granted by the province of Nova Scotia to tiiis railway. The arbitrators did not proceed on any other ground as will be perfectly evident to any one who will examine the award. I can see no distinction between the case of the province and that of the municipalities. They seem to be precisely in the same category, namely, that this government, having become possessed of a railway, which railway has been constructed in part by subsidies from the province of Nova Scotia, and in part by subsidies from the municipalities, the Dominion should therefore refund, to the province and the municipalities the amount so expended. It is perfectly clear to any one who looks through the verbiage of this award that this is the principle upon which the arbitrators proceed. That being so, there can be no justification for refusing a reference of the claims of the municipalities, and there can be no reason for distinguishing their case from that of the province.

If there is anything clear on the face of this award it is that the arbitrators have determined that there has been a clear breach of contract between the government of Canada and the government of Nova Scotia, and that whether or not the measure of damages is such as to commend itself entirely to their judgment from a legal point of view, the arbitrators, had power by reason of this reference to fix and determine, themselves, what the amount of damages should be according to any measure that commended itself to their judgment. But, my hon. friend cannot dispute the proposition that they recognized the liability of the Dominion to make compensation to the government of Nova Scotia, because the government of Canada had made a contract with the government of Nova Scotia which they had not performed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I can only repeat what I have already said that I do Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
not find a single fact stated on the face of this award which would justify the awarding of this sum of $671,836 as the measure of damages for the breach of contract. That is my view. It may not be the hon. gentleman's view, and if it is not there is no use of us discussing it. I understand the hon. Solicitor General to concur in the view which I have expressed to the committee, that the arbitrators have proceeded, not on that ground at all. They have proceeded on the equitable ground, which is, that the province of Nova Scotia having spent $670,000 and upwards on this railway are entitled to get it back. All I have suggested is that if it is proper under the circumstances to refer that matter to the arbitrators and to pay the amount of their award to the province, it is only right to deal in the same manner with the municipalities which have made a similar contribution.

The hon. gentleman is all wrong in his statement. It is stated in so many words that the reason why the arbitrators gave compensation at all to the province is because of the breach of contract. They have given that measure of damages and they are estopped from going the length of the full measure they could go, because the full measure I presume would be the restoration of the rights of which the province was deprived under the contract. So many things have happened since, that it was impossible to do that, but the measure of damages is given which it is reasonable that the Dominion should pay.

I do not want to take up the time of the committee by prolonging this discussion, but I say there is nothing on the face of the award to show that the province has lost five cents by reason of the breach of contract. But there is something in the award which shows that the province has expended $670,000 on this railway, and It is upon that ground that the arbitrators have gone in deciding the measure of damages, and not upon the question of the breach of contract.

My hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) says that the award does not show that the province of Nova Scotia has lost five cents by reason of the breach of contract. What is shown in the award is that by the breach of contract the province of Nova Scotia has failed to become the owner of the road as under the contract it should have been.
The province of Nova Scotia might become the owner of the road, and be much worse off.
That is not my contention.

Does not my hon. friend, as a lawyer, understand that

any person making a claim for breach of contract must show actual damages, otherwise he will recover merely nominal damages. I am not criticising this. I am only saying that the award really proceeds, not on the ground of breach of contract, but on the ground that the province expended a certain amount of money to get the railway, and that it is therefore entitled to get that money back.
If there had been no question of breach of contract the same award would have been given ?
Yes, I think so. I think the same award might have been given if there had been no breach of contract.

I think my hon. friend (Mr. Borden. Halifax) and I will agree, that if we were to proceed with this matter in court he and I would probably understand one another better. Under such circumstances the action would have been to set aside the contract. If proceedings had been taken you would have proceeded for a breach of the contract, distinguishing between the breach and the measure of damages. The breach is the starting point, and the measure of damages is the consequence. So, you deal with that breach of contract here ? Where is the breach ? The breach of contract entered into between the government of Nova Scotia and the government of Canada. Now, the municipalities cannot come in there, because we have no contract with them. The measure of damages contemplated here comes as a result of the violation of this contract; but you cannot deal with the municipalities on that basis, because you are without your premises. Your conclusions are all right, but your premises are all wrong, because the contract is wanting in the case of the municipalities. I think when we come to talk law we understand one another better.
* Mr. BORDEN (Halifax). I do not have the slightest difficulty with the hon. Solicitor General. I only suggest that when you come to deal with this breach of contract, and when you come to consider what are the damages consequent upon it, you will find nothing on the face of the award which will show damages there in the sum claimed. My hon. friend and I are at one on that. I simply go a step further and say that looking at the award in that light you will see that it Is plain that the arbitrators simply took into consideration the subsidy which the province had granted.
The arbitrators have not proceeded on the ordinary rules of law, but as the arbitrators put it in foro conscientiae.

Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) affirm that the arbitrators have not explicitely declared that there was a violation on the part of the government of its contract with the province of Nova Scotia ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I have not said anything of the kind.

Then, my hon. friend's observation, made in the light of that fact, can have no possible application to the case of the municipality which has no contract with the Dominion government, and which, therefore, has no possible cause of action against it in respect to such railway. My hon. friend's argument that it does not appear that there has been any clear, or what he would call from a legal point of view, well defined measure of damages, concluded upon by these arbitrators, is a proposition entirely out of the question.
They affirm that there was a contract upon certain conditions. They affirm in so many words that when the time came for carrying out that contract the Dominion government used its force by duress to compel the government of Nova Scotia to submit to conditions which were not in accordance with the original contract. Having forced an unwilling acquiescence from the government of Nova Scotia, they followed that up by saying : We regard the amount which was contributed by the government of Nova Scotia as a fair compensation to that government from the government of Canada, which has done this wrong. You may turn or twist it in any way you please, but there is the connection clear and plain. I dissent from the proposition of my hon. friend who is holding out to the people of Nova Scotia an invitation to come to this government, or to some succeeding government with a demand to pay the interest on this amount. There is no basis for that proposition. The two parties agreed to a solution of this controversy by submitting it to arbitration, and whether Nova Scotia got little or much, or capital or interest, or neither, they can make no further claim with respect to this matter in the future. I am sorry to hear my hon. friends opposite make suggestions which will encourage demands that they know have no foundation in law or justice.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I must not allow to pass uncorrected the statement of the Minister of Railways. I see no reason stated on the face of this award for denying interest to the province. I say that if a further reference were made in the terms of this present reference, the province of Nova Scotia would be permitted to go behind this award in the matter of a claim for interest. This reference says that the arbitrators are not bound by the strict rules of law. and if those words were included in the further reference, they could go behind this award upon a claim for interest, just as under this reference the arbitrators have gone behind

the agreement made between the province and the Dominion of Canada. That is all I meant.

The Sth paragraph of the submission to the arbitrators states that they are to decide if such claim should be allowed, and, if so, whether they should be allowed the interest from the date of the demand. Therefore, the arbitrators passed on that claim for interest, rejected, and disposed of it. The question was included in the arbitration proceedings.

I was led to make the statement I did because I do not find any adequate ground disclosed for refusing interest. What I say is, that if any similar reference were made in the future it would just be as competent for arbitrators to go behind this award as it was for these arbitrators to go behind the contract between the province and Canada. That seems to be the case. I have great respect for the opinion of the Solicitor General, and if he will say that is not the case I may feel bound to reconsider my opinion'.
What my hon. friend says is, that if the claim for interest were submitted by agreement between the parties they might do so. That would go as a matter of course.

We have had a very lengthy legal argument from gentlemen on both sides, but I wish to draw the attention of the members of this House and of the people of this country to the very little that ordinary members of parliament have to say in matters of this kind. The Minister of Finance taunted us this afternoon that we had acceded to many appropriations and that we did not challenge them by a vote. What chance has the opposition got to oppose an item of this kind. What had the members of this House to say in the matter before it was submitted to arbitration. The claim came from the lower provinces by interested parties, the government arranged for an arbitration, and they now come with the results of that arbitration to force it through the House. They have already pledged the honour of the country to pay the money. The taunt of the Minister of Finance was undeserved by us, and was unworthy of him. What chance had the opposition to criticise this matter except from the legal point of view, and so far as that goes the gentlemen on the Treasury benches got very much the worse of the argument.
Hear, hear.

I can understand the leader of the government laughing at the ignorance of a layman, but I can tell him that the people of this country will look at this matter as I do. Perhaps the Minister of Finance could taunt his own followers. We have been here for over three months, and

we have had very few remarks from the members supporting the government and certainly never a dissent to( what the government does. What is the use of recording a vote on a matter of this kind ? We cannot stop it passing. Can the leader of the House show me how it is possible for us to block a deal of this kind going through. If he can show me I will be very glad to do it. It may be desirable for political reasons to pass this vote, but on the equity of the case the government has not a leg to stand on. I would not be at all afraid even in the absence of any legal knowledge, to meet the Minister of Finance-probably not in his own province but in any county in Ontario- to discuss this matter with him, and 1 think he would fail to convince the people that there was any fair chance for the opposition to prevent the passage of this vote through the House of Commons. Let the Prime Minister show how we can block a deal of this kind. If he does I will endeavour to block it. In view of that condition of things I again repeat that the taunt of the Finance Minister was neither fair nor just.

There is only one way and it is a very easy way. We submit this vote to parliament but the hon. gentleman (Mr. Brock) is not bound to accept our views. Of course the minority has to be bound by the decision of the majority, but there is a way in which the hon. member can protect himself; that is, to challenge this appropriation by a vote of the House. Then he will show before the House and the country what is his position and the position of his friends upon it.

There is a sophistry there. The hon. Prime Minister knows what chances we have in a vote of this House at the present time. When he says that we can challenge a vote of this House, he knows the solid voters which he has behind him, who would express an opinion one day in one direction and come into this House the next day and vote in the opposite direction.
My hon. friend knows also that if there is a solid vote behind us, there is a solid people behind us both to which he can appeal.

I am sorry that the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) took so much to heart my observations of this afternoon, which he has repeatedly characterized as taunts. I thought they were very moderate, not such as to give offence, and entirely in the line of legitimate criticism. I agree with my hon. friend on one point; we are both laymen, and are therefore apt to be confused by the lawyers' statements of this question. But so far as it is discussed, I am going to rely on the layman's view of it. I think this question has been made so plain by the arbitrators that the wayfaring

man, though a layman and a member of parliament, can understand it. I agree with my iron, friend that those who do not understand the matter thoroughly have not much chance of going into the 'history of this transaction and ascertaining it thoroughly from A to Z; and if I should go with him into the province of Ontario, where he seems to think the standard of criticism and intelligence is somewhat different from a similar standard in the maritime provinces -though I do not know why he should think so-and if I were to discuss this question with him there, I would not expect, in the ordinary time which would be given to me at a public meeting, to make all the citizens who might be iiresent understand it all; but I would expect to tell the audience in Ontario that an independent board of arbitrators, headed by a distinguished jurist from the province of Ontario, who had all the facts before them, had investigated the matter in every mood and tense of it, with the advantage of able counsel on both sides who understood the matter, and had given judgment; and I would ask the intelligent people of Ontario to accept that judgment, though they might not accept mine, nor the judgment of my hon. friend from Centre Toronto. This question came up as a claim from the present government of Nova Scotia; but inasmuch as it dealt with transactions which arose at a time when I myself was a member of the government of Nova Scotia, I felt from the beginning that I should not take a very prominent part in it. I realized that I should probably be called as a witness; and so I said to my colleagues in the ministry here, after I obtained their concurrence in the view that the matter should be referred for inquiry to an independent tribunal, that I wished to have no part in it, and that whatever was necessary for the presentation of the Dominion side would be dealt with by others, who would take advantage, of course, of any information that might be available in my department. So, realizing that I might be called as a witness, X took no part in the matter. The history of this case is a long one, and if any one were to take some isolated part of it, as some hon. gentleman opposite have done, he might find himself in error. But every fact stated, every passage read, every matter brought forward here to-night was fully placed before the arbitrators, and whatever force It was entitled to it received at their hands; and now we have their judgment before us.
Not all. The hon. gentleman's speech was, but that was all.

I do not know how my hon. friend gets that. I know I was examined and cross-examined on that speech by the able counsel who represented the Dominion. Now. I want to give a brief statement of what I call the 186
layman's view of this transaction. The I'ictou Branch Railway, as it is calld, the branch in question, cost about $2,000,000. It is not to be confused with the Pictou town branch, built in later years. Sometimes the property in question is called the Truro Branch and sometimes the Pictou Branch. It is a line running from Truro to New Glasgow and to the waters of Pictou Harbour. It was the avowed policy of. all parties in this House, as far back as the seventies, to give up that branch for the purpose of assisting railway construction eastward. Whether or not that was a wise policy is not worth our while to debate. Originally a resolution was moved in this House by the late Mr. Justice Macdonald, at the time the member for Antigonish, recommending that that branch be set apart for that purpose. Ultimately an Act of parliament was passed setting apart that branch to be given for the assistance of railway construction eastward from New Glasgow. A contract was made between the government of Nova Scotia and a company headed by Sir Hugh Allan for the construction of the Eastern Extension Railway, on two conditions: first, a subsidy of $8,000 a mile, and secondly, the grant of this Pictou branch, which had cost upwards of $2,000,000. That branch was given up for that purpose, and virtually ceased to be the property of the Dominion government. The Allan Company built their road, 80 miles in length, relying on getting this Pictou branch as part of the consideration. There was in the tripartite agreement a condition, that if the company should fail to complete their contract, their property should pass into the hands of the local government, and if the local government should fail to operate the road effectively, it should pass into the hands of the Dominion government. The local government obtained that road, not by way of forfeiture, but by negotiations with the Allan Company. The government of that day, of which Sir John Thompson was Attorney General, entered into an arrangement with the Allan Company. whereby it consented that within a certain time this Pictou branch and the new road should pass into the hands of the local government. But though the local government of that day made that agreement with the Allan Company, they did not follow it up immediately by legislation. When in 1882 a new administration came into power, that agreement was brought to their notice -it was not at that time on the public files of the province-and it was then found that the local government had the right to acquire the Pictou branch and the Eastern Extension from the company within a given time. There was no legislation of a provincial character to raise money for that purpose, and the local government experienced some embarrassment as to how to deal with it. There were some negotiations with the Dominion government as to the



possibility of tbeir taking it over in trust or otherwise; but tbe Dominion government declined to have anything to do with it. When the local legislature met, it provided that the government might borrow money for the necessary expenditure, under an arbitration to determine what was the company's outlay in excess of the subsidy. That arbitration was held, the amount due the company was awarded, and arrangements were made for the purchase. That was done by legislation of the local legislature in 18S3. The local government were proceeding on the assumption that the new road was not in itself a profitable investment, at that time at all events, whatever its future prospects might be; but the basis of the arrangement was getting possession of the Pictou branch along with the new road; and before they would put a dollar into the enterprise, although they had taken legislative authority to do so, they sent delegates to Ottawa to place the matter before the Dominion government to see that there would be no trouble on that score. The delegates came here, brought their Bill, submitted it to the Dominion government, and asked the Dominion government to give their immediate assent to it; that is, that the question, of disallowance should be determined at once, instead of being allowed to stand for a year, as is usual, and that they should declare by order in council that the Act would not be disallowed, but should immediately go into operation. That step was taken, so that the Dominion government did not then contemplate any difficulty about the delivery of the branch. Sir Charles Tupper was then Minister of Railways, and he discussed the question with the delegates. He said to them :	The property is yours,
you are entitled to get it just so soon as you take possession of the new road. This is what he said, as reported in ' Hansard' ;
The committee was aware that, under the legislation which had already taken place, the government of Canada agreed to hand over the branch from Truro to Pictou for the purpose of securing the construction of a line eastward, and the government of Nova Scotia, with an additional subsidy, secured the construction of a line to the Strait of Canso. Under the existing legislation, the whole of that property is, therefore, the property of the Eastern Extension Company.
Observe, it was no longer the property of the Dominion.
But the government of Nova Scotia made a contract with that company which bound the company, in case the government by a certain time paid them their actual expenditure, to hand over to the government of Nova Scotia the whole property. It is expected that in a few days the road from Truro to the Strait of Canso will be in possession of the government of Nova Scotia, and the government of Nova Scotia are anxious to utilize that for the purpose of securing the extension of the railway system to Sydney in Cape Breton.
Thus, the consent of the Dominon was given cheerfully to the legislation of the

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: province. We had the admission of Sir Charles Tupper, then Minister of Railways, that the branch had ceased to be the property of the Dominion, and had passed into the control of the Eastern Extension Company, which had transferred it to the government of Nova Scotia, and that in a few weeks the government of Nova Scotia would enter into possession. Relying on that, the local government sent their agent to England to arrange to borrow the money required. They committed themselves to a large expenditure, which they would never have dreamt of doing if they were not to obtain the Pictou branch as well as the new road. The arrangements went on until October. They took possession of the Eastern Extension property. They paid the money in accordance with the contract, and wrote to Ottawa to get possession of the Pictou branch, according to the law, and the understanding, and everything fair and reasonable. But the Dominion government refused. They gave no explanation or reason, but simply a flat refusal. Then the delegates came to Ottawa and asked for an explanation. It was long before they got any, and finally they obtained an order in council, setting forth that the property would be given over to them on certain conditions. The whole thing turns on the terms of that order in council. If it was a legal and proper order in council, then the Dominion was in the right. If it was illegal and improper, then the arbitrators have given a right decision in the matter. What were the terms of the order in council ? It declared, first, that the government of Nova Scotia must equip the road with a large amount of rolling stock. Hon. gentlemen have said that the Nova Scotia government were bound to have the road efficiently equipped. That is true, but, what is an efficient equipment ? The local government had provided that which they were advised by a competent railway engineer was a sufficient equipment ; and when the demand was made that they should put a larger equipment on the road, it was quite evident that the object was to impose a condition which would prevent their taking it over.

What did Mr. Schreiber have to say when examined ?
Mr. HACIvETT. What was the date of the order in council ?

The 20th of October, 18S3. The Nova Scotia government made this proposal. They said that they did not admit the right of the Dominion government, at that stage, to dictate what was a proper equipment. They said that that question might come up later; but, in order that it should not be dealt with in a technical spirit, in order to take what the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Brock) would call a layman's view of the matter, they 'said ; You ask us to put a certain equipment on the road, which our engineer

says is not necessary, we will refer tlie matter to three independent railway experts, and if they say that move rolling stock is required to efficiently operate the road, we will put it on. But, the Dominion government said : No, you must take our decision.
The hon. gentleman will not say that that came out in evidence.
That is beyond dispute.
It does not appear in the evidence.

It is not a matter of dispute. The correspondence showed that the Nova Scotia government were willing to call in independent experts, and that if these experts said that the equipment furnished by the local government was not sufficient, the Nova Scotia government would put on more. But, that government objected to being obliged to put on a quantity of rolling stock, which their own engineer advised them was excessive. The position taken by the local government was a fair and reasonable one.
The other condition was as regards the tariff. Our hon. friends opposite say that there was a condition obliging the Nova Scotia government to operate the road at a fair and reasonable tariff.
Has the hon. gentleman a copy of the order in council ? It has not been printed.

The order in council of 1883 ? It is in the hands of the Solicitor General. The next question was with regard to the tariff. My hon. friend from Bothwell assumed that the local government had taken a most extraordinary position in that matter. I am satisfied that I can convince even him that the attitude of the local government on that question was a very fair one. What was the demand of the Dominion government ? It was, first, that you shall prepare a tariff at once. The local government replied : No, the moment has not arrived. We will take over that road and operate it under the existing tariff, and then prepare a tariff, under the terms of the Act, and submit it to you ; and when we do that, we are willing to discuss with you what is a fair and reasonable tariff. But, the Dominion government insisted : No, law or no law, you must agree on a tariff now. The Nova Scotia government refused, and the arbitrators have said that the demand was an illegal one.
The hon. gentleman will surely not say that any evidence was given to guide the arbitrators to that decision ?

All the documents containing that fact will be found attached to the reports of the arbi-186* .
trators, because they are too important to be overlooked. The Dominion government not only insisted on a tariff being settled at once, but undertook to stipulate what that tariff should be. There is nothing in the Act which provides that the Dominion government shall prepare the tariff and fling it at the local government and say : You must adopt it. The Act says that a fair and reasonable tariff shall be submitted for the approval of the Dominion government.
In the first stage of the business, if the company had operated the road according to the tripartite agreement, the approval of the tariff would not have been in the hands of the Dominion government at all, but in the hands of the local government, and only in the event of a dispute between the local government and the government should the Minister of Public Works be called in as arbitrator. But, there was another stage. The road passed from the company into the hands of the local government, and the local government recognized that, as owners of the road, they did not occupy an independent position, and were prepared to submit a tariff for the approval of the Dominion government. But, the Dominion government said :	We will make a tariff
now, and you must accept it or nothing. You must like it or lump it.

The hon. gentleman is stating the case from his own point of view, and putting it as unfavourably, from the Dominion government point of view, as he possibly can. I do not think that the Dominion government could have used the language he attributes to them.
I am putting the case as a layman to another layman.
You are not putting it fairly, but emphasizing it in the wrong way.
The hon. gentleman has no right to say that. I have read the documents and he has not.
The hon. gentleman quotes the Dominion government as saying : You can either like it or lump it.

They did not dot their I's and cross their T's just in that way, but that was the substance of what they said. They said : We will impose a tariff, and if you do not accept it, you cannot get your property. And I translate that freely to say : You may like it or lump it-and every layman in this House will agree with me. Now I am going to ask my hon. friend from Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) to agree with me, because I know that, though he is a strong party man, this point is so strong
I am not aware that there is any party politics in this question at all.

I withdraw that remark, I did not wish to wound my hon. friend. But, unfortunately, sitting on that side of the House my hon. friend is so prone to see things differently from the way we see them, and there must be some reason for it. But I wish to ask his attention to the next point as to the tariff that was provided. This branch from Truro to Pictou was about 40 or 45 miles long ; and the Dominion made this cool proposition, that we of the local government-for I was a member of it-should accept a tariff rate per ton-mile on that short haul of 40 miles the same as on the long haul of 800 or 900 miles of the Intercolonial Railway. That is, every ton carried over the 40 miles of that road should pay only the same rate per mile as was paid by every ton carried over the Intercolonial Railway.
Was not that the rate they were paying on that line ?
They were running it as a branch of the Intercolonial Railway.
In the interest of the people.

We are not discussing that. Of course all these things are done in the interests of the people. But this road belonged to the local government, according to Sir Charles Tupper, who dealt with the matter frankly and fairly. It was the right of that government to operate the road on the same terms as anybody would operate a road of 40 miles, and when the Dominion government made this demand that the same ton-mile rate should be charged as on the Intercolonial Railway, they made a demand that, my hoti. friend (Mr. Brock) will agree, was unjust and at variance with every principle of railway management known in this country. Will he agree with me in that ? Would he expect a little road of) 40 miles running out of Toronto to give him the same mileage rate as a great through line' of 1,000 miles ? He knows that such a thing is preposterous. If he were the owner of such a road and any one made a demand of that kind, he would make up his mind that that person did not wish to do business and he would leave him. I know, that I have his sympathy in that. The local government said : What is the use of keeping up this fight ? There may have been reasons for the Dominion government's action, possibly reasons related to the local interests of the counties. But whatever they were, the Dominion government said in effect: We do not intend to give you the property. And the local government, making the best of a. bad business, made an agreement that the Dominion should be allowed to take over the road on paying the same sum that the local government had paid to the Allans, about $1,200,000. The correspondence will show that again and again the demand Mr. BROCK.
was made for the subsidy. My hon. friend from Bothwell said that at no time were the local government anxious to get the road. Of course, he was mistaken. I know that the local government sent its members to kick their heels about Ottawa for two or three weeks at a time beseeching the Dominion government to give them the road. The local government passed an Act to raise the money to obtain the road. The local government appointed men to manage it, and they took over the eastern extension and had it in their possession. Surely the hon. gentleman cannot be serious.

The hon. gentleman was in the local legislature and took a prominent part in the whole negotiations, in fact, one of the most prominent. He must have sat very close to his leader, and his leader declared that the object of getting the Dominion government to take over the road and operate it for two years was to convince the province that it was not in their interest to have the road.

Even if any individual said that, it would prove nothing. The local government passed legislation, borrowed money, employed men to operate the road, sent delegates here to Ottawa-did everything to get the road. Whether it was a good or a bad policy was not the question-it was their property and they had the right to it. They made the best of a bad bargain when they went back to the legislature. They were violently attacked by their opponents who said that they	should	not	have given up theroad.	They	made	the	best defence theycould. Take the whole debate through, and all the papers through, and it will be found that the spirit running through the whole thing	was	that the	local governmentmade every honest effort to get the Pictou branch,	while	the	Dominion government determined they would not give it, and, that being the case there was no use in trying to get it. Even if they had their legal rights, the local government might be embarrassed a great deal. This road was important in its connection with Cape Breton and Prince Edward Island, but it had to rely for its connection with the railway system of the continent upon the Intercolonial Railway which was managed by the Ottawa government. And if the Ottawa government were determined to act in an unfriendly spirit, clearly, the local government would not have much satisfaction in operating the road. The whole question is whether the order in council of 1883 was a proper interpretation of the agreement and the Acts of parliament. If it was, it is of no consequence to look at any other phase of the matter ; if it was a proper interpretation, the local government have no right to complain. That is the point that was referred to the arbitrators. They were able men. My hon. friend the Prime Minister has re-
*59-29

ferred to Chief Justice Burton. The others were Mr. Barbeau, of Montreal, and my hon. friend the present member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade)-though, not at the time of his appointment a member or candidate. These gentlemen went into the matter thoroughly. The Dominion had the benefit of the services of a very able lawyer, Mr. Lafleur, who did everything he could to maintain the interests committed to his charge. I know that he did his part in cross-examining me as a witness, and I honour him all the more for it. After going through the whole matter the arbitrators came to the conclusion, and reported, that the conditions laid down on the 20tli October, 1883, were not fair or reasonable conditions to carry out the spirit of the Act, but they were conditions which must have been made to frustrate the intention of the Act and prevent the local government from obtaining possession of its property. That is the crux of the whole business. If that order in council was fair, the local government have no claim. If it was unjust or unreasonable, net Intended to carry out the delivery of the road, but to prevent the local legislature from getting the property, it was a breach of contract and a great wrong. And, no matter what any individual may have said in trying to make the best of a bad bargain the fact remains that the wrong was done, and the arbitrators have so found it. In view of all the facts, the arbitrators decided that the order in council of 20tli October, 1883, was unjust, it was illegal, and, in consequence of that unjust and illegal Act the province should i-eceive compensation in the shape of a return of the subsidy it had paid for this extension. The Dominion government have already paid $1,200,000, and. if this award is acted upon and the amount paid, they will pay an additional $071,000. That is, the Dominion government will have paid a total of $1,871,000. For what ? For two roads which cost $4,000,000.
The province of Nova Scotia was recouped for that under the arrangements made for confederation.

What has that to do with the question ? That pi dee of railroad was the property of the Dominion of Canada down to the year 1S70. Nobody disputes it, the Dominion owned it. The Dominion by an Act of parliament passed that over to the company, and through the company to the local government. Now, there is no use going behind that. It was Dominion property, they voted it away from their possession, and we have this statement of Sir Charles Tupper made in the House of Commons :
Under legislation the whole of that property is therefore the property of the Eastern Extension Company, but the government of Nova Scotia made a contract with the company

And so forth, showing that the government of Nova Scotia acquired the company's
rights. Therefore, by the confession of Sir Charles Tupper, that was the property of Nova Scotia. They were illegally kept out of that property, and in consequence this award has been made. Now, coming back again to the layman's view, that property cost $4,000,000. But no matter what it cost it was property owned by the government of Nova Scotia. That property owned by the government of Nova Scotia costing $4,000,000 passed into the hands of the Dominion government, and all they will have paid for it, including this award, will be $1.S00,000. So they will then have obtained $4,000,000 worth of property for which they have paid only that sum.
Was that amount you speak of charged to the province of Nova Scotia before confederation ?

This Pictou railroad was in course of construction at the time of confederation, and was finished about the time of the union. No doubt it entered into the general financial relations between the province and the Dominion. But it passed out of the control of the Dominion just as much as a barrel of fish would pass out of the control of my hon. friend when he had sold it. It no longer belonged to the Dominion, it belonged to the province of Nova Scotia. Upon the faith of that pledge they borrowed that money, upon the faith of that pledge they did everything. It was their property, they had a right to if, and when they did not get possession of it they had a just claim against the Dominion government. The arbitrators, who were honourable men, who had more time to go into it than we had, who investigated the matter from beginning to end, and who surely had no desire to do anything but what was right and just for the whole Dominion, have decided that this sum should be paid.

The. committee will be surprised at the hon. gentleman who, after a very eloquent speech, has sat down without uttering one word to show that Nova Scotia has suffered any damage. No hon. gentleman has ventured to say that she has. Under all the circumstances. Nova Scotia having given a subsidy, they must have some excuse for getting it back.
That was precisely the matter which was referred to the arbitrators, and they decided it.

My hon. friend knows that it is unfair to urge that the country has to accept and reverence a judgment because It came from respectable men. Respectable men in this country more than once have given judgments that eminent lawyers have dissented from, and that the courts have reversed on appeal. So I think it is unfair to urge any such consideration.

Nobody questions their respectability, but respectability has never on all occasions proved to have given judgments that are eitjier wise or prudent.

Prince Edward Island paid for its own railway. Now the government is asked to refund to Nova Scotia an amount of money expended since confederation on railways. I would like to ask whether, if you commence refunding to the provinces money spent on railways before or since confederation, you should not consider the case of a province that built its own railroads before confederation ?

I now understand my hon. friend's question better than I did at first. The money which was expended by the local government, and which was the subject of this award, was not paid before confederation, but was paid many years after confederation, out of the local treasury, and had no relation to the terms of confederation.

We have been treated to a long speech by the Minister of Finance. The ground that he has taken, apparently, is that this whole question was referred to independent arbitrators, and .we have the result of their decision. What kind of an arbitration -was it with Nova Scotia on the one side, pressing their claims as strong as they could, and the other side represented by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding), who has just taken his seat.

I was not representing the other side. I stated at the beginning that I had nothing to do with the Canadian side of the question. It was understood I was representing the province of Nova Scotia, and I told my right lion, friend the premier from the beginning, that I was not in any way to have anything to do with the management of the Canadian side.

Who was it secured a reference to arbitration ?
The minister of finance. The
whole government, and to that I was a party.	'
On whose recommendation ?
On recommendation of the Prime Minister of Canada.
On recommendation of the Minister of Finance, in the first instance.
I was a party to it with all my colleagues. The only recommendation was the recommendation of the Prime Minister.
Was it not a matter that came within the jurisdiction of the Minister of Finance ?

Not particularly. A deputation came from the government of Nova Scotia and appeared before the whole council, and stated the case again and again, and the Prime Minister himself reported, for the particular reason that I did not feel, as Minister of Finance, that I was the man to manage the Canadian side of the case.

As a matter of fact, here we have the evidence that on one side was the government of Nova Scotia pressing the claim, and on the other side was the government of Canada in full sympathy with the claim.
That has not appeared.
Yes, it has appeared, it has appeared from the speech of the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat.
No, I say I wasi in sympathy with the claim.
The hon. gentleman was in sympathy with the claim, and it was made a strong election card in the province of Nova Scotia.
No, I never alluded to it in any shape or form.

I am not speaking of the hon. gentleman. I say it was made a strong election card in Nova Scotia. The late Minister of Justice, Sir John Thompson, declared that was no legal claim, and I would accept the dictum of Sir John Thompson, as a jurist, in that matter before I would that of any one else I know of, because he knew all the circumstances of the case. He was a native of Nova Scotia, he was in the legislature, he was a judge, then he came here as Minister of Justice, he was in close touch with all the proceedings from the start; almost right up to the time he died. Sir John Thompson declared there was no legal claim whatever. Then what was there to refer to arbitrator's ? I say you cannot get away from the fact that you have on one side the parties pressing their claim, and on .the other side, instead of a party opposing it, you have a party in fullest sympathy with it. The Minister of Finance himself was in full sympathy with it.

My hon. friend should not say I was on the Canadian side of the case, because I have told him again and again that I had nothing to do with the management. I did not even know who the counsel was until after he was employed.
In the first place, he was a member of the government of Nova Scotia, that had long pressed the claim.
Yes.

Then he became a member of the government whose duty it was, supposedly, to resist the claim, else why did they refer it to arbitration ? Why didn't they investigate the claim as a government and say :	Yes, you have proved your claim,
and we will pay it without referring it to arbitration, without goiug through the farce of an arbitration. Then what does this open the door to ? The leader of the opposition has said that the claim for interest appears to him to be just as strong as the claim for principal. We will have, presumably, In the future, a claim made lor interest. If the claim is as strong, why should it not be made ? Then, we have the claims of the municipalities. The award does not say that the damages granted are for a breach of contract, but these damages are given because the province paid out money and we have to recoup it for the money paid out. If it he the case that the municipalities have equally as strong a claim as the Nova Scotia government to which we are paying $071,000, and we may have a further claim for interest we will have the municipalities putting in another claim, because, under the decision of the arbitrators, they have equally as strong a claim as the Nova Scotia government. Then, where will it end ? The province of Nova Scotia comes along with its claim and it will be said that the Dominion government is ready to recoup us; we will go to it with our unsound financial enterprises and hand them over to the Dominion. The claim of the province of New Brunswick amounts to $285,000, $148,000 of principal, and the balance in interest, and this claim is to be paid. Then, the province of Prince Edward Island comes along under the plea that during the years from 1S73 to 1870, the contract with them was not carried out. Hon. gentlemen opposite were in power during the whole of that period except perhaps a few months in 1873. I will not be certain about that. They did not keep up communication between the island and the mainland according to the terms of the agreement with that province. We had a claim settled the other day by this Liberal government, and this Liberal parliament which seems ready to vote everything through without any investigation. The Chairman was not able to read the item out until we had a chorus of voices declaring it to be carried. It is a scandal and a farce to say that this is legislation and that we are here to make investigations into the expenditure of the country. The clamour of the majority of this House prevents even a semblance of an investigation being made. Then the right hon. leader of the government comes along and asks: Why do you not take a vote ? Why do you rot call in the members and decide it in that way ? There is a better way than that, and it is to investigate the matter. You call in the members and vote it down. Unless
you express your dissent it does not give the people the reason for your objection to the claim. We have had the hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart), the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy), and other hon. gentlemen going into the history of the case, but in the view of the right hon. gentleman, there is nothing in it at all. His argument is:	Call in the members.
They will decide the matter. Mr. Chairman, that will not go down -with the people of this Dominion. They want to have an investigation. They want to know what are the reasons for these things, and yet the only reply is :	Why do you not call
in the members. We have called in the intelligent jury of the public. The case has been stated from this side of the House, and we have had a confession from the non. Minister of Finance wTho is the ardent advocate to-night of the claim of Nova Scotia, as he was when he was the premier of Nova Scotia, and was advancing this claim against the Dominion government. I rely, so far as the legal points are concerned, upon the decision, after the fullest investigation into the facts, of the late Sir John Thompson who said that there was no legal claim.
IV lie re does that appear ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I think I heard the hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) state that in the House to-night. Of course we have not all the information because the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals has refused to put documents on the Table of the House that we should have. Where is the order in council relating to that matter ?
Here it is.
It has been on the Table of the House for a fortnight.
And printed by order of this parliament.
No, the order in council has not been printed.
Yes, I have it here.
No, but I mean the order in council in reference to the alleged breach of contract.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Wallace) asked for the order of reference.
No, I asked for the order in council.
My hon. friend (Mr. Haggart) had the order in council.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: No.
It is amongst the papers.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I handed *them over to the hon. Solicitor General.
Well, the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals has been asked for the order in council and it has not been placed on the Table of the House.
Yes, it has been placed on the Table of the House.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I do not say that it has not been placed on the Table of the House. I got the whole of the papers, but I did not know that the order in council was amongst them. I handed them to the hon. Solicitor General.
That was last night. The hon. gentleman has had them for a week.

The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals has been asked for the order in council, we have been unable to procure it, and we are told now that the hon. Solicitor General has it. Why should it not be printed and distributed amongst the members ? Surely an important document like that, having reference to a vote of $671,000, should be available for the members of the House instead of being given to any one member to look at. It is not the $671,000. It is the fact that further claims may be made upon this parliament upon the strength of the payment of this $671,000, because other provinces may bring in claims equally as strong if not just on all fours with this one which is a complicated arrangement. They may be able to bring in much stronger cases probably than is presented to us on this occasion. We are spending the money-$671,000 to Nova Scotia, $285,000 to New Brunswick. making about $1,000,000, and $30,000 a year to Prince Edward Island, the interest on a million dollars at 3 per cent. The province of Ontario may come in on the strength of this, and inay present claims to the amount of $1,000,000. The province of Quebec may come along with its claims in the same way because the door has been opened.

May I suggest to the right hon. leader of the government that when papers relating to important matters of this kind are laid on the Table of the House a little care should be taken by some officer of the government to see that the necessary documents are brought down and printed ? It turns out that this order in council is a most important document.
I have searched the statutes of 1883 and 1884 to find it, and I have not been able to get it. However, it turns up now.
Here it is.

Never mind about it now ; I am only stating that in the future I think some competent person might be instructed by the government to look after papers and see what are necessary for thet purpose of an intelligent discussion of the subject dealt with, and let these be printed and placed in the hands of hon. members.
In reference to the papers they have absolutely all been brought down. There are three or four volumes of them. Nothing could be more complete than what I have brought down.

The papers were brought down and they were ordered to be printed. I supposed they contained all that was necessary for an intelligent discussion of the case, but now it ajjpears that is not the case. I do not blame my right hon. friend, but, I say that in future some competent person should look over these papers beforehand, and see that everything is included which is necessary for an intelligent discussion.

This is sessional paper 73, and it is prepared for printing, not by a clerk, but by a committee of the House.
Mr. BORDEN (Halifax),. Then, let it be considered their fault.

The proper question for discussion is, whether this government acted rightly in submitting this matter to arbitrators. There was a contract between the Dominion government and the province of Nova Scotia, and if disputes arose in reference to this contract, surely that is a proper subject for arbitration. I rise in order to dissent, and to put on record my dissent, to the propositions laid down, not very strongly indeed, but rather intimated, by the leader of the opposition. He stated that the door is opened to municipalities to claim from the government because of subsidies they have granted. Well, there is no contract between these municipalities and the Dominion government, and, therefore, there is no ground on which they can make a claim against the Dominion government. The leader of the opposition also stated that there is an open door left for a claim for interest, but he rather withdrew' that, although it was repeated by his first lieutenant (Mr. Wallace) and sometimes leader, who sits to his right. I dissent from that proposition as strongly as I can. The whole claim of the province, whatever it may be, wTas referred to the arbitrators, and they have decided on that whole claim. There is a finality in reference to these awards, and in some respects they are even stronger than the decisions of the courts. It seems to me altogether wrong to intimate that there is any chance of Nova Scotia coming back here and claiming interest, Of course, it goes without saying.

that if the Dominion government agreed of Its own accord to refer anew a claim for interest, arbitrators might have the power to deal with it, but no one supposes that when governments have submitted a matter for arbitration and an award has been made, that they are going to make another reference of a claim for interest. It is rather amusing to hear these gentlemen opposite say that they are not opposing this on party grounds, and especially so in the case of the member for Toronto (Mr. Brock). Why, every question is a party question with him.
Not at all.

When the hon. gentleman (Mr. Brock) -was a candidate in Toronto, he had the temerity to say that all the Liberals were hypocrites, and it took him all the rest of the campaign to explain that statement.
It was so true that I am elected.
The hon. gentleman from Kingston (Mr. Britton) does not understand the argument. Does he mean to say that the arbitrators decided that there was a breach of contract and assessed damages ?
Yes.

Well, he is the only one in the House who thinks that. There is no evidence that there was any damage done to the province of Nova Scotia, and the arbitrators do not say anything of the kind in their award. We complain that there was no rule to guide the arbitrators and so they adopted the rule of thumb. Under the same principle it is set out in this reference, every municipality in the country would be entitled to recover under a similar claim. The member for Bothwell touched the pit of the argument when he pointed out that not one member of parliament, from the Prime Minister down, attempted to say that there was the least damage done to the province. The fact is, that the province entered into a contract to build a railroad, and the railroad was taken over by the Dominion, much to the delight of the province, because they got the road better equipped and the rates lower than if the province operated the road. The hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Britton) said there was a finality to this, and that there could be no further claim for interest. Why the very next item is an award for interest just under similar circumstances to this one. He is making an excellent argument against the next item. The Finance Minister threw the taunt across the floor of the House that the opposition did not challenge a vote on any of the items in the estimates except one.
That is the sort of argument which might be used on the stump. Has the hon. gentleman ever had the pleasure of an intimate acquaintance with the proceedings of the British House of Commons ? Did he ever 'listen to the remark of the Right Hon. Joseph Chamberlain when a gentleman in his constituency challenged him for having allowed certain votes to pass without dividing the House upon them ? In the British House of Comons, as in the parliament of nearly every country, it is sufficient for the opposition to protest without dividing the House ; and a first-class statesman, a man who occupies a prominent position in any parliament, never divides the House in committee. If the matter is of sufficient importance, he makes his motion before going into committee, and divides the House then. But for these items the responsibility is entirely on the government, and it is sufficient for the opposition to protest against them, without dividing the House. Such an argument as the hon. Finance Minister has used is only wliat he might use when he is stumping Queen's and Shelburne, but it is not consonant with the dignity of a Finance Minister addressing the House.
It might go in Ontario.

I can tell the hon. gentleman that it is sufficient in our province for the people to know that we have protested all we could against this expenditure. The hon. member for Kingston says that this decision is a finality. But when he comes to the next vote, for New Brunswick, he will find that there is no finality to anything. He will be astonished at his own argument in this case, for he will find that we not only pay the award, but that a long time afterwards a demand is made upon us to pay the interest on the amount that we thought was a finality at the time. There is nothing to prevent the province of Nova Scotia, now that the governmefit acknowledges its claim, coming back in the future and demanding interest on the ground that we had already admitted the principle. That is the result of all these little deals. It is extraordinary that three of them should crop up at one time, just before an election-one in Nova Scotia, one in New Brunswick, and one in Prince Edward Island. Prince Edward Island seems to have got far the best of the bargain-$070,000 for Nova Scotia : $280,000 for New Brunswick, but $1,000,000 for the tight little Island of Prince Edward. Where does the rest of the Dominion come in ? That is what we are objecting to. If you are going to have rearrangement of the subsidies, there ought to be a fair share all round ; and you cannot expect gentlemen from other provinces to look with anything but jealousy on these arrangements with Nova Scotia. New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. We have had brilliant surpluses for the last few years -nearly $20,000,000 raised from the people of the country, and expended where ? Part

of it to the Intercolonial Railway, and the balance, I suppose, as additional subsidies to these two or three provinces, and my poor native province without anything at all. I see that British Columbia is getting jealous. It is sticking its oar in if there is to be a distribution. But I am afraid that if there is a fair distribution Ontario will prefer to drop its portion of the plunder and leave the matter where it is.

I wish to make a few remarks on this subject notwithstanding the lateness of the evening and the dying hours of the session ; and I propose to do it now, especially in view of the taunts thrown across the floor of the House so often that we have not entered our protest against any of the proposed items of expenditure. This Is, in my judgment, another raid on the treasury in the dying hours of the session, when less than half the members of this House are here to consider the question, the other half having gone home to attend to their duties, supposing the work of the session was over. By actual count a few minutes ago I found that there were exactly 65 members in this Chamber. That represents one-third of the House.
The MINISTER OP MARINE -AND FISHERIES. There were 151 here a short time ago.

In the first place, I think the practice is wrong of submitting these items for our consideration at this late stage of the session. In the next place these items are evidence to us that there has been a concerted action in the maritime provinces to make another raid on the treasury of the country. We have heard rumours for some years past, and have seen them frequently denied by friends of hon. gentlemen opposite in the press, but now they have culminated in these appropriations. The arbitration on this transaction I regard as an arbitration voiced from one side and not from the other. It suggests to us this question : Will there ever be a finality in the financial arrangements between the provinces and the Dominion V We were assured in 1S84 that we had then reached a finality, when the Hon. Mr. Blake said : ' If there is not a finality on these claims on the Dominion, the result must be to break up confederation.'
That had nothing to do with claims at all. He was speaking of the rearrangement of the subsidies.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
The rearrangement of the subsidies based on the claims being made, with the possibility of other claims being made in the future. A rearrangement was made at that time, and amounts were voted that were thought to be sufficient. But it seems that we have not reached that finality yet ; and from what has occurred this session, there seems no reason to hope Mr. HAGGART.
that it will be reached in the near future ; for there is just as much reason for other provinces to apply for additional subsidies as the provinces which are now being recouped.
We have not a word of protest from the Ontario members supporting the government. The only one among them who opened his mouth on this vote is the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Britton), and he volunteered a defence that was neither legal nor equitable, but political. I do not propose taking up time by going into the merits or demerits of this claim, but only wish to draw attention to the fact that the supporters of the government from Ontario. Manitoba, the North-west Territories, and British Columbia, instead of being here doing their duty on behalf of their respective provinces, are absent, witli the exception of a few who are prepared to allow the Minister of Finance to go it blind. The great province of Ontario, which is the milch cow of confederation, is being milked again, and there is not a member from that province supporting the government independent enough to enter liis protest. As soon as the item was called, I noticed these hon. gentlemen clearing out from the House, as they always do whenever there is a critical vote about to be submitted, so that they may afterwards plead as an excuse: I did not happen to be present when this expenditure was brought down.
We have this item of $671,836 for Nova Scotia, and that is to be immediately followed by another one of $280,692 for New Brunswick, and we have given practically a million dollars to Prince Edward Island. These three provinces ought to be satisfied. What guarantee have we that Quebec will not come next and that Manitoba and the North-west Territories and British Columbia and Ontario will not each follow in turn with a claim of a similar nature ? If there is one thing more than another calculated to break up confederation, it is these perpetual demands on the Dominion treasury.
Has the hon. gentleman's leader repudiated this transaction ?
Had the hon. gentleman been in his place, he would have heard what the leader of the opposition said.
I was in my place, and heard what he said.
Has the hon. gentleman himself said one word against it ?
Certainly not. Has the leader of your party said a word against it?

Certainly he has, and if the hon. gentleman had been in his place, as he should have been, he would have heard what the leader of the opposition said. Have any of his friends from Ontario said a word against it ? Not one.

They are willing to vote it without examination or inquiry. The item was hardly read before they all began Co cry out carried.
What particular item does the hon. gentleman take objection to ?

I am taking objection to the item proposed to be voted now. Does the hon. gentleman know what it is ? He ought to have been in his place and knqwn what was being submitted to the House. I rose to enter my protest, and I say the principle is wrong. The arbitration was largely a one-sided one. These repeated demands from the provinces will lead to trouble in the future as they are doing now. These hon. gentlemen went to the people of the maritime provinces, upon the strength of what they could get from the government, and they are now delivering the goods to the best of their ability.
Might I ask the hon. gentleman if he is thoroughly endorsed by his lender in the remarks he has made?
I am expressing my own views, and that is quite enough for me, and if the hon. gentleman would give expression to his, he would be doing better than trying to cross-examine me.

Are you endorsed by your leader in the remarks you made ? You are a prominent member of your party, are you endorsed by your leader ?
To provide for payment of award of arbitrators in connection with Eastern Extension Railway, New Brunswick, 5148.96S.75; for interest on same from July 1, 1884, to July 1, 1901, $126,623.43, and costs of reference, $5,100, $280,692.18.

I do not think the facts could be stated any more clearly than they are in the award of the abritrators, which is not a very lengthy document. This claim arises out of the construction of the Intercolonial Railway about the time of confederation. The New Brunswick government had contracted to build a piece of road which afterwards passed over to the Intercolonial Railway. The commissioners of the Intercolonial Railway-that road was then in the hands of a commission-agreed to take the road off the hands of the company at a valuation, which was supposed to bear a relation to the cost of constructing the lines of the Intercolonial Railway in the same section, near the boundary line between Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. The estimated cost of construction of the Intercolonial Railway in that region was therefore the basis of the arrangement made by the commissioners of the Intercolonial Railway. when taking over this piece of road. The local government had contributed a certain subsidy to the road. They received part of that snbsidy back at the time out of the sum then paid. But it subsequently transpired that the estimated cost of the constructipn of the Intercolonial Railway in that region was far below the actual cost. When the New Brunswick government found that the cost of constructing the new portion of the Intercolonial Railway in that region was greater than the original estimate, they came to the Dominion government and said : You based your payment for the New Brunswick section on the estimated cost of construction approved by the commissioners, but you must give us an additional amount based on the actual cost.
Is the hon. gentleman in possession of the documents that he makes reference to ?

Yes, but I cannot tell why the document was not sooner in the hands of hon. members. There seems to have been some delay in the printing. The Dominion government years ago acknowledged the propriety of the New Brunswick government's contention. They acknowledged that the property should have been taken over at a valuation, based upon the actual cost of construction of the new work on the Intercolonial Railway, and not the estimated cost. The Dominion government paid the local government $150,000 in recognition of that claim, that being the difference between the first valuation of the road and the second. From that time the local government have been contending for the interest. The argument of the province, and it was reasonable, was that if they were entitled to that money, they were entitled to it under an arrangement [DOT]about 1809, and if it had been placed to their credit in 1869, they would have received half-yearly, as part of their annual allowance, the interest on that sum. But it was not placed to their credit till many years after. The claim that they make is that they are entitled to that interest from the time when the sum should have been placed at their credit. It was thought well not to determine this claim by the government here, but to refer it to arbitration. The arbitrators were Mr. Justice Barker, of New Brunswick: Mr. Justice Lan-gelier, of the province of Quebec ; and Mr. Duncan Coulson. general manager of the Bank of Toronto. These gentlemen investigated the matter and came to the conclusion that the claim of the New Brunswick government was a fair and reasonable one. That, in brief, is a statement of this claim.	.

It seems perfectly clear that New Brunswick had subsidized the road to the extent of $400,000. Although a settlement was made at the estimated cost and $250,000 was placed at the credit of the province to recoup it for its ex-

penditure, the claim was made for the balance of $150,000. I shall not take up time by discussing the arguments, the reasons and no reasons, put forward in support of that claim. The amount was paid by a subsequent arrangement. So where are we now? We are asked to do what the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Britton) told us in unequivocal terms could never be considered-to give interest upon a claim that was supposed to be settled. This means, as the hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) has pointed out. Nova Scotia has a right to demand, on the same basis as that upon which this claim is allowed, that before this parliament rises interest shall be paid upon the sum which lias just been voted to that province. There is absolutely no difference between the cases. No training, no legal Ingenuity will enable any hon. gentleman to make a distinction between them. I will not detain the committee, but I wish to enter my protest against this dangerous system. If we hope to have confederation a success, we must have honourable, upright and manly partners in it.
